arXiv:2503.20620v1 [math.GR] 26 Mar 2025

Combination theorems for Wise’s power alternative

Mark Hagen Address: (Mark Hagen) School of Mathematics, University of Bristol, Bristol, UK Email address: markfhagen@posteo.net , Alexandre Martin Address: (Alexandre Martin) Department of Mathematics, Heriot-Watt University and Maxwell Institute for Mathematical Sciences, Edinburgh, UK Email address: alexandre.martin@hw.ac.uk and Giovanni Sartori Address: (Giovanni Sartori) Department of Mathematics, Heriot-Watt University and Maxwell Institute for Mathematical Sciences, Edinburgh, UK Email address: gs2057@hw.ac.uk
Abstract.

We show that Wise’s power alternative is stable under certain group constructions, use this to prove the power alternative for new classes of groups, and recover known results from a unified perspective.

For groups acting on trees, we introduce a dynamical condition that allows us to deduce the power alternative for the group from the power alternative for its stabilisers of points. As an application, we reduce the power alternative for Artin groups to the power alternative for free-of-infinity Artin groups, under some conditions on their parabolic subgroups. We also introduce a uniform version of the power alternative and prove it, among other things, for a large family of two-dimensional Artin groups. As a corollary, we deduce that these Artin groups have uniform exponential growth.

Finally, we prove that the power alternative is stable under taking relatively hyperbolic groups. We apply this to show that various examples, including all free-by-ℤ\mathbb{Z} groups and a natural subclass of hierarchically hyperbolic groups, satisfy the uniform power alternative.

1. Introduction

1.1. Motivation

We say that a group GG satisfies the power alternative (or Wise’s power alternative in [55]) if, for every g,h∈Gg,h\in G, there exists n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that either gng^{n} and hnh^{n} commute or they generate non-abelian free group. This alternative is closely related to the Tits alternative for non-positively curved groups, and Wise asked whether all CAT⁡(0)\operatorname{CAT}(0) groups (or non-positively curved groups in a broader sense) satisfy it [18]*Question 2.7. While Leary and Minasyan recently provided the first example of a CAT⁡(0)\operatorname{CAT}(0) group not satisfying the power alternative  [51]*Example 9.4, this alternative has been established for many non-positively curved groups by various means. For example, in 1979, Jaco-Shalen proved a strong form of the power alternative for G=π1​MG=\pi_{1}M where MM is an atoroidal Haken 33–manifold [48]*Theorem VI.4.1. If GG is a hyperbolic group, standard arguments provide some n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G, either ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅ℤ\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong\mathbb{Z} or ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2} [53]*Theorem 8.3.13. For GG a right-angled Artin group, Baudisch proved that the power alternative holds for GG with n=1n=1, that is, two elements of a right-angled Artin group either commute or generate a non-abelian free subgroup [9]. In particular (see Lemma 2.2) the power alternative holds for virtually special groups in the sense of [45], which implies the power alternative for Coxeter groups, among many other examples (see Section 6). The power alternative for right-angled Artin groups also implies that same alternative for mapping class groups, by work of Koberda [49]*Corollary 1.2. Very recently, the power alternative has been established for mapping tori of many injective free group endomorphisms, and thus many free-by-ℤ\mathbb{Z} groups [3].

Artin groups form a large class of groups generalising braid groups, and which are conjectured to be non-positively curved in some sense. It is thus natural to ask:

Question 1.1 ([55]*Question 1.2).

Which Artin groups satisfy the power alternative?

Recently, Antolín and Foniqi proved the power alternative for even Artin groups of FC-type [5]*Theorem 1.1, and Martin proved it for two-dimensional Artin groups of hyperbolic type [55]*Theorem B. In this article, we prove the power alternative for new classes of Artin groups.

In a different direction, it is natural to ask whether the power alternative is stable under various group constructions. Antolín–Minasyan proved that the power alternative is stable under taking graph products of groups [7, Corollary 1.5]. In this article, we obtain several new combination theorems for the power alternative. That is, given a group action on a simplicial complex, we provide conditions on the action so that the power alternative for stabilisers of simplices implies the power alternative for the whole group. We investigate in particular groups that arise from fundamental groups of graphs of groups (via their action on the associated Bass–Serre tree) and relatively hyperbolic groups (via their action on their coned-off Cayley graph). We thereby obtain a collection of combination theorems that recover several of the above results in a unified way, and allow us to obtain new ones.

1.2. Splittings and applications to Artin groups

For a group acting on a tree, we first investigate when it is possible to derive the power alternative for the group from the power alternative for the stabilisers of points. Note that this does not hold in full generality: For instance, the Baumslag–Solitar group BS⁡(1,2)\operatorname{BS}(1,2) can be written as an HNN extension of the form ℤ∗ℤ\mathbb{Z}*_{\mathbb{Z}}, and in particular acts on a tree with infinite cyclic point stabilisers, yet it does not satisfy the power alternative. In a different direction, the power alternative is still open for groups acting geometrically on a product of two trees, due to the presence of antitori [67]. These groups decompose as fundamental groups of graphs of free groups, and as such act on simplicial trees with free groups as the cell stabilisers (see Example 4.13).

We introduce a stabilisation property (see Definition 3.4), which is a condition on the dynamics of the action that allows us to derive the power alternative for the whole group. This condition is in particular satisfied by acylindrical actions, see Example 3.5.

Our main criterion is the following. We phrase it for actions on simplicial trees as our applications deal with such actions, but the theorem holds more generally for actions on real trees:

Theorem A (power alternative for actions on trees).

Let TT be a simplicial tree and let GG be a group acting on TT via graph automorphisms. Let us further assume that:

  1. (1)

    for every x∈Vert⁡(T)∪∂Tx\in\operatorname{Vert}(T)\cup\partial T, the power alternative holds for StabG⁡(x)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x);

  2. (2)

    the action G↷TG\curvearrowright T has the stabilisation property (see Definition 3.4).

Then the power alternative holds for GG.

We also obtain a more algebraic version of this criterion, where the condition on the stabilisers of points at infinity is replaced with a condition on stabilisers of points and certain associated “mapping tori”, see Corollary 4.8.

As an application, we first study Artin groups. It is known that if the presentation graph of an Artin group is not a complete graph, then the group admits a visual splitting as an amalgamated product of standard parabolic subgroups (see Section 4.4). We obtain the following general result:

Corollary B.

Let AΓ=AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ2A_{\Gamma}=A_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{2}} be an Artin group expressed as a visual splitting with the following properties:

  1. (1)

    the power alternative holds for the factors AΓ1A_{\Gamma_{1}} and AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{2}};

  2. (2)

    AΓA_{\Gamma} has the parabolic intersection property and the normaliser structure property (see Definition 4.17).

Then the power alternative holds for AΓA_{\Gamma}.

The parabolic intersection property and the normaliser structure property are conjectures about parabolic subgroups of Artin groups that are believed to hold for all Artin groups. So far, they have been proved only for certain sub-classes (see Section 4.4 for more details). Under the assumption that these two conjectures hold, Corollary B reduces the power alternative for all Artin groups to the power alternative for Artin groups over complete graphs (the so-called free-of-infinity Artin groups), see Corollary 4.22.

1.3. The uniform power alternative

In this article, we introduce a natural quantitative strengthening of the power alternative: We say that a group GG satisfies the uniform power alternative if there exists a uniform integer N∈ℕ≥1N\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that, for every g,h∈Gg,h\in G, either [gN,hN]=1[g^{N},h^{N}]=1 or ⟨gN,hN⟩G≅F2\langle g^{N},h^{N}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2}. This is strictly stronger than the power alternative (see Example 2.3), and holds for hyperbolic groups, right-angled Artin groups, and virtually special groups, for instance.

Although it is straightforward to produce examples of groups that satisfy the power alternative but do not satisfy the uniform one, we do not know whether the two properties are equivalent for finitely-presented groups, whence the question:

Question 1.2.

Is there a finitely-presented (torsion-free) group that satisfies the power alternative but does not satisfy the uniform power alternative?

Dihedral Artin groups are known to satisfy the power alternative with a uniform exponent that only depends on the associated label [46]*Lemma 4.3. We exploit this result to verify the uniform power alternative for a wide class of two-dimensional Artin groups, and with a uniform exponent that depends only on the set of labels of the presentation graph:

Theorem C.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group whose defining graph is (2,2)(2,2)-free and triangle-free. For each edge {a,b}\{a,b\} of Γ\Gamma with label ma​bm_{ab}, let

ma​b′={ma​b/2if ma​b is even2​ma​bif ma​b is oddm_{ab}^{\prime}=\begin{cases}m_{ab}/2&\text{if $m_{ab}$ is even}\\ 2m_{ab}&\text{if $m_{ab}$ is odd}\end{cases}

and let N=lcm⁡{ma​b′:{a,b}∈Edge⁡(Γ)}N=\operatorname{lcm}\left\{m^{\prime}_{ab}:\{a,b\}\in\operatorname{Edge}(\Gamma)\right\}. The following holds:

  • •

    if N≥3N\geq 3, then AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the uniform power alternative with exponent NN.

  • •

    if N=2N=2, then AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the uniform power alternative with exponent 44.

The uniform exponent defined in Theorem C is optimal in the first case. In the second case, the expected optimal uniform exponent would be N=2N=2, however our approach yields a strictly larger constant in that case (see Lemma 5.16, whose proof requires a constant at least 33).

If all the labels are even, then an Artin group AΓA_{\Gamma} as in Theorem C is an even FC type Artin group. The above theorem is thus related to Antolin–Foniqi’s “strongest Tits Alternative” for these groups [5]*Theorem 1.1. Indeed, one of the consequences of their main result is that such an Artin group AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies a uniform power alternative with exponent N≔∏Edge⁡(Γ)ma​b′N\coloneqq\prod_{\operatorname{Edge}(\Gamma)}m_{ab}^{\prime}. The exponent provided in Theorem C is sharper (optimal, in most cases) and independent of the size of Γ\Gamma.

As a corollary, we prove that the Artin groups considered in Theorem C have a uniform exponential growth, in the following strong sense:

Corollary D.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a triangle-free (2,2)(2,2)-free Artin group that is not of spherical type. Let mm be a uniform exponent for the power alternative for AΓA_{\Gamma} (as defined for instance in Theorem C). Let SS be a generating set of AΓA_{\Gamma}. Then there exist s,t∈Ss,t\in S such that sms^{m} and tmt^{m} generate a non-abelian free subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}. In particular, AΓA_{\Gamma} has uniform exponential growth.

1.4. Relative hyperbolicity

In Section 6, we consider the (uniform) power alternative for relatively hyperbolic groups, deducing the power alternative for the whole group from the power alternative for the peripheral subgroups. Our main result is the following:

Theorem E (Theorem 6.9).

Let GG be a finitely generated group that is hyperbolic relative to a finite collection 𝒫\mathcal{P} of subgroups. Then GG satisfies the power alternative provided each H∈𝒫H\in\mathcal{P} does. Moreover, if each H∈𝒫H\in\mathcal{P} has bounded torsion and satisfies the uniform power alternative, then GG satisfies the uniform power alternative.

This generalises the well-known fact that hyperbolic groups satisfy the uniform power alternative (see Theorem 6.5). Our proof is phrased as much as possible in terms of acylindricity of the action of GG on the coned-off Cayley graph, and we imagine that there might be a larger class of acylindrically hyperbolic groups for which one can deduce the (uniform) power alternative from the assumption that a sufficiently rich class of elliptic subgroups satisfy the power alternative uniformly. In Section 6.4, we ask some questions about an analogue of Theorem E for various hierarchically hyperbolic groups. In this direction, Definition 6.3 specifies classes of groups shown in Theorem 6.4 to satisfy the power alternative (uniformly). These classes are constructed from some initial groups by closing the class under various operations: passing to finite-index subgroups and overgroups; direct products and graph products more generally; acylindrical graphs of groups; relatively hyperbolic overgroups with the given groups as peripheral subgroups. A concrete example is the class one gets starting with hyperbolic groups.

As a concrete application of the results in this section, we analyse 33–manifolds and free-by-cyclic groups; for instance, we use structural results about mapping tori, due to many authors, to apply our combination theorems to prove the following:

Corollary F (Corollary 6.20).

Let FF be a finite-rank free group and Φ∈Out⁡(F)\Phi\in\mathrm{Out}(F). Then G=F⋊ΦℤG=F\rtimes_{\Phi}\mathbb{Z} satisfies the uniform power alternative.

In [3, Theorem B], it is shown that if Φ\Phi is fully irreducible and x,y∈Gx,y\in G, then ⟨x,y⟩\langle x,y\rangle is either free, free abelian, the Klein bottle group, or has finite index in GG, all of which imply the uniform power alternative. It does not appear that the results in [3] imply that conclusion without the full irreducibility hypothesis, however, so the above corollary seems new. Examining the constants in the proof shows that the uniform exponent depends only on rk⁡(F)\mathrm{rk}(F) provided the relatively hyperbolic structure from [33] can be chosen so that the hyperbolicity and acylindricity parameters are bounded in terms of rk⁡(F)\mathrm{rk}(F). Such bounds do not immediately appear in [33], but François Dahmani has explained in personal communication that there are good heuristic reasons to think they should exist.

1.5. Organisation of this paper

In Section 2 we introduce the power alternative and its uniform version. Section 3 is devoted to proving our criterion for proving that a group satisfies the power alternative, that is, Theorem A. In Section 4 we list some examples (and non-examples) of groups that satisfy the power alternative with a particular focus on Artin groups expressed as a visual splitting. In section 5 we prove that (2,2)(2,2)-free triangle-free Artin groups satisfy the uniform power alternative, with uniform exponent depending only on the set of labels of a defining graph. Finally, in Section 6 we study the stability of the power alternative under the construction of relatively hyperbolic groups. In particular, we prove that relatively hyperbolic groups satisfy the power alternative, if every peripheral subgroup does.

1.6. Acknowledgements

We would like to thank María Cumplido for helpful discussions on the normalisers of parabolic subgroups of Artin groups and François Dahmani for explaining relative hyperbolicity constants in mapping tori.

2. Preliminaries on the Power Alternative

In this section, we recall the definition of the power alternative and introduce its uniform version, and prove some preliminary results about them that are used throughout this paper.

Definition 2.1 (power alternative).

Let GG be a group.

  1. (1)

    We say that GG satisfies the power alternative if, for every g,h∈Gg,h\in G, there exists n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that either gng^{n} and hnh^{n} commute or ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2};

  2. (2)

    Let n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}. We say that GG satisfies the nn-uniform power alternative or the power alternative with uniform exponent nn if, for every g,h∈Gg,h\in G, either gng^{n} and hnh^{n} commute or ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2};

  3. (3)

    We say that GG satisfies the uniform power alternative if GG satisfies the nn-uniform power alternative for some n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}.

It is straightforward, yet very useful, to observe that the power alternative can be detected from finite-index subgroups:

Lemma 2.2.

Let G,HG,H be groups, let G′≤GG^{\prime}\leq G be a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to a subgroup of HH.

  1. (1)

    If HH satisfies the power alternative, then GG satisfies the power alternative;

  2. (2)

    If HH satisfies the power alternative with uniform exponent nn, then GG satisfies the power alternative with uniform exponent n⋅|G:G′|n\cdot\lvert G:G^{\prime}\rvert.

Example 2.3.

The uniform power alternative is strictly stronger than the non-uniform one. For instance, let GG be an infinitely generated torsion group with the property that, for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, there exists an element of GG of order nn. Then GG satisfies the power alternative but with no uniform exponent in general.

Also observe that the (uniform) power alternative is stable under direct products:

Lemma 2.4 (stability under direct product).

Let G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} be groups.

  1. (1)

    If G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} satisfy the power alternative, then so does G1×G2G_{1}\times G_{2};

  2. (2)

    If G1G_{1} satisfies the mm-uniform power alternative and G2G_{2} satisfies the nn-uniform power alternative, then G1×G2G_{1}\times G_{2} satisfies the power alternative with uniform exponent lcm⁡(m,n)\operatorname{lcm}(m,n).

Proof.

Let G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} satisfy the power alternative. For i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, let πi:G1×G2→Gi\pi_{i}\colon G_{1}\times G_{2}\to G_{i} denote the projection on the ii-th factor. Let (g1,g2),(h1,h2)∈G1×G2(g_{1},g_{2}),(h_{1},h_{2})\in G_{1}\times G_{2}. If there exist i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that ⟨gin,hin⟩Gi≅F2\langle g_{i}^{n},h_{i}^{n}\rangle_{G_{i}}\cong F_{2}, then ⟨(g1,g2)n,(h1,h2)n⟩G1×G2\langle(g_{1},g_{2})^{n},(h_{1},h_{2})^{n}\rangle_{G_{1}\times G_{2}} is non-abelian free as well. If there are n1,n2∈ℕ≥1n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that [g1n1,h1n1]=[g2n2,h2n2]=1[g_{1}^{n_{1}},h_{1}^{n_{1}}]=[g_{2}^{n_{2}},h_{2}^{n_{2}}]=1, then, by choosing nn as the least common multiple of n1n_{1} and n2n_{2}, we have that (g1,g2)n(g_{1},g_{2})^{n} and (h1,h2)n(h_{1},h_{2})^{n} commute. The uniform case is analogous. ∎

3. Groups acting on trees and the power alternative

In this section, we prove a geometric criterion for a group acting on a tree to satisfy the power alternative, namely the stabilisation property from Definition 3.4.

Theorem 3.1.

Let GG be a group acting by isometries on a real tree TT, such that the action satisfies the stabilisation property. If stabilisers of all points of T∪∂TT\cup\partial T satisfy the power alternative, then so does GG.

Theorem A, which is stated for our main case of interest, i.e. actions on simplicial trees by graph automorphisms, follows from Theorem 3.1:

Proof of Theorem A.

In order to show that the action G↷TG\curvearrowright T satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, it suffices to show that stabilisers of points of TT satisfy the power alternative. Let x∈Tx\in T. Then StabG⁡(x)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x) has a subgroup of index at most 22 that sits as a subgroup of a vertex-stabiliser [63]*Section 3.1, so Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 3.1 imply the theorem. ∎

3.1. Action on trees and fixed point sets

We recall the definition of real trees and establish some graph-theoretic notation.

Definition 3.2 (real trees).

A metric space TT is a real tree (or ℝ\mathbb{R}-tree) if the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    for each pair of points x,y∈Tx,y\in T there exists a unique geodesic segment [x,y][x,y] connecting them;

  2. (2)

    for all points x,y,z∈Tx,y,z\in T, if [x,y]∩[y,z]={y}[x,y]\cap[y,z]=\{y\}, then [x,y]∪[y,z]=[x,z][x,y]\cup[y,z]=[x,z].

As a standard example, a simplicial tree, together with its path metric where every edge is given length 11, is a real tree. For a survey on non-simplicial examples, see [17]. A real tree TT is in particular Gromov-hyperbolic, and we denote as usual by ∂T\partial T its Gromov boundary.

Isometries of a real tree TT are either loxodromic or elliptic (see e.g. [31, 1.3]). For a loxodromic isometry gg, we denote by Axis⁡(g)\mathrm{Axis}(g) the unique axis of gg, and by τ⁡(g)>0\tau(g)>0 the translation length of gg on its axis. For an elliptic isometry gg, we denote by Fix⁡(g)\mathrm{Fix}(g) the corresponding fixed-point set, which is a ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle-invariant and closed convex subset of TT.

The following notion will play a key role when studying the subgroups generated by large powers of two isometries of TT:

Definition 3.3 (stable fixed-point set).

If g∈Gg\in G is an elliptic element for the action G↷TG\curvearrowright T, then the stable fixed-point set of gg is defined to be

Fix∞⁡(g)=⋃x∈⟨g⟩−{1}Fix⁡(x),\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)=\bigcup_{x\in\langle g\rangle-\{1\}}\operatorname{Fix}(x),

which is a ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle-invariant and convex subset of TT.

We introduce a property that allows us to get some control on stable fixed-point sets.

Definition 3.4 (stabilisation property).

Let TT be a real tree and let GG be a group acting on TT via isometries; we say that the action G↷TG\curvearrowright T has the stabilisation property if the following condition holds: Let {γn}n≥1\{\gamma_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} be a sequence of geodesics of TT that is monotonic for the inclusion, that is, γn⊂γn+1\gamma_{n}\subset\gamma_{n+1} for all nn, or γn+1⊂γn\gamma_{n+1}\subset\gamma_{n} for all nn. For each n≥1n\geq 1, let ℓ⁡(γn)∈ℝ≥0∪{+∞}\ell(\gamma_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\cup\{+\infty\} denote the length of γn\gamma_{n}, and let HnH_{n} denote the point-wise stabiliser of γn\gamma_{n}. If ℓ⁡(γn)→+∞\ell(\gamma_{n})\rightarrow+\infty, then the sequence {Hn}n≥1\{H_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} of subgroups stabilises, that is, there exists an integer N≥1N\geq 1 such that Hn=Hn+1H_{n}=H_{n+1} for all n≥Nn\geq N.

Example 3.5.

If a group GG acts acylindrically (see Definition 6.1) on a real tree TT, then the action has the stabilisation property, since there exists a uniform constant LL such that any geodesic segment of length at least LL has finite pointwise stabiliser.

Example 3.6.

For an example of an action that does not satisfy the stabilisation property, consider the Baumslag–Solitar group BS(1,2)=⟨a,b|bab−1=a2⟩\operatorname{BS}(1,2)=\langle a,b~|~bab^{-1}=a^{2}\rangle, expressed as the HNN extension ⟨a⟩∗⟨b⟩\langle a\rangle*_{\langle b\rangle}, with Bass–Serre tree denoted TT. Then the geodesic ray γ\gamma of TT spanned by the vertices b−n​⟨a⟩b^{-n}\langle a\rangle, for n≥0n\geq 0, has pointwise stabiliser ⟨a⟩\langle a\rangle, and for every n≥1n\geq 1, the translate bn​γ⊃γb^{n}\gamma\supset\gamma has pointwise stabiliser ⟨a2n⟩\langle a^{2^{n}}\rangle.

3.2. Proof of Theorem 3.1

In this subsection we will prove Theorem 3.1 by analysing the dynamics of elements gg and hh on the tree TT: for a pair g,h∈Gg,h\in G, we shall study the subgroup ⟨gn,hn⟩G\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}, depending on whether gg and hh act on TT both elliptically, both loxodromically or in a mixed fashion.

Lemma 3.7 (elliptic-elliptic case).

Let the group GG act by isometries on the real tree TT. Suppose g,h∈Gg,h\in G act elliptically, and that Fix∞⁡(g)∩Fix∞⁡(h)=∅\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(h)=\varnothing. Then ⟨g,h⟩≅⟨g⟩∗⟨h⟩\langle g,h\rangle\cong\langle g\rangle*\langle h\rangle.

We will use the following elementary observation:

Lemma 3.8.

Let TT be a real tree, and consider a closed path in TT that decomposes as the concatenation γ1∪⋯∪γk\gamma_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\gamma_{k} of kk geodesic segments γ1,…,γk\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{k} of TT (concatenated in the given order). Suppose that the overlaps between consecutive γi\gamma_{i}’s are such that for every 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, we have

γi′≔γi−(γi−1∪γi+1)≠∅\gamma_{i}^{\prime}\coloneqq\gamma_{i}-(\gamma_{i-1}\cup\gamma_{i+1})\neq\varnothing

(with the convention that γ0=γk+1=∅\gamma_{0}=\gamma_{k+1}=\varnothing). Then the geodesic segments γi\gamma_{i} are pairwise distinct (as subsets of TT).

Proof.

We leave it to the reader to check by induction on kk that the closures of the γi′\gamma_{i}^{\prime} concatenate into a non-backtracking path of TT (hence a geodesic of the real tree TT), and that for each 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, the geodesic γi′\gamma_{i}^{\prime} belongs to γi−∪j≠iγj\gamma_{i}-\cup_{j\neq i}\gamma_{j}. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.7.

Let γ\gamma be the unique geodesic in TT between the closed sets Fix⁡(g)\operatorname{Fix}(g) and Fix⁡(h)\operatorname{Fix}(h). Let w=w0w1⋯wkw=w_{0}w_{1}\cdots w_{k} be a non-empty reduced word in the alphabet {g,h}\{g,h\}, where w0=1w_{0}=1 and the wiw_{i}’s are alternating non-trivial elements of ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle or ⟨h⟩\langle h\rangle for i∈{1,…,k}i\in\{1,\dots,k\}. To prove that ⟨g,h⟩=⟨g⟩∗⟨h⟩\langle g,h\rangle=\langle g\rangle*\langle h\rangle, it is enough to show that ww acts as a non-trivial isometry of TT. For each ii, let

γi=⋃i=0kw0⋯wi⋅γ\gamma_{i}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{k}w_{0}\cdots w_{i}\cdot\gamma

We claim that for every ii, the interval γi−(γi−1∪γi+1)\gamma_{i}-(\gamma_{i-1}\cup\gamma_{i+1}) is non-empty. Indeed, up to translation, this amounts to checking that the interval γ−(Fix⁡(αi)∪Fix⁡(βi))\gamma-(\operatorname{Fix}(\alpha_{i})\cup\operatorname{Fix}(\beta_{i})) is non-empty for some suitable non-trivial elements αi∈⟨g⟩\alpha_{i}\in\langle g\rangle and βi∈⟨h⟩\beta_{i}\in\langle h\rangle, and this follows from the assumption that the stable fixed-point sets are disjoint. It now follows from Lemma 3.8 that the γi\gamma_{i} are pairwise distinct. In particular, γ0=γ\gamma_{0}=\gamma and γk=w⋅γ\gamma_{k}=w\cdot\gamma are distinct, hence ww acts non-trivially on TT. See Figure 1 for an intuition. ∎

Lemma 3.9 (mixed, bounded case).

Let TT be a real tree and let GG be a group acting on TT by isometries. If g∈Gg\in G acts elliptically on TT, h∈Gh\in G acts loxodromically on TT and Fix∞⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h) is bounded (including the case where it is empty), then there is n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that

⟨g,hn⟩G≅⟨g⟩G∗⟨hn⟩G.\langle g,h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong\langle g\rangle_{G}*\langle h^{n}\rangle_{G}.
Proof.

Let π:T→Axis⁡(h)\pi:T\to\operatorname{Axis}(h) be the closest-point projection map and let A=π⁡(Fix∞⁡(g))A=\pi(\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)), which is either a single point or equal to Fix∞⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h) if the latter is nonempty. Let K=|A|K=\lvert A\rvert, which is finite by assumption.

Let z∈Fix⁡(g)z\in\operatorname{Fix}(g) and let p=π⁡(z)p=\pi(z) and let D=dT​(z,p)D=d_{T}(z,p). For any k≠0k\neq 0, consider π⁡(gk​Axis⁡(h))\pi(g^{k}\operatorname{Axis}(h)). Either this is a single point, or it is equal to gk​Axis⁡(h)∩Axis⁡(h)=Bg^{k}\operatorname{Axis}(h)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h)=B. In the latter case, let x∈Bx\in B. Then [z,x]=[gk​z,x][z,x]=[g^{k}z,x] passes through pp since x∈Axis⁡(h)x\in\operatorname{Axis}(h) and through gk​pg^{k}p since x∈gk​Axis⁡(h)x\in g^{k}\operatorname{Axis}(h) and gk​pg^{k}p is the projection of gk​z=zg^{k}z=z onto gk​Axis⁡(h)g^{k}\operatorname{Axis}(h). Since dT​(z,gk​p)=Dd_{T}(z,g^{k}p)=D, we have p=gk​pp=g^{k}p, i.e. p∈Fix⁡(gk)∩Axis⁡(h)p\in\operatorname{Fix}(g^{k})\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h). Thus g2​k​x=xg^{2k}x=x and hence x∈Fix∞⁡(g)x\in\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g). We have shown that π⁡(gk​Axis⁡(h))\pi(g^{k}\operatorname{Axis}(h)) has diameter at most KK for all k≠0k\neq 0, and moreover it is contained in the KK–ball about the point pp, which is independent of kk.

Now consider ∂T\partial T, equipped with the usual visual metric. We have just shown that there are open sets U±⊂∂TU^{\pm}\subset\partial T, respectively containing h±h^{\pm}, such that gk​{h±}∩(U+∪U−)=∅g^{k}\{h^{\pm}\}\cap(U^{+}\cup U^{-})=\varnothing for k≠0k\neq 0.

On the other hand, ⟨h⟩\langle h\rangle acts on ∂T\partial T with north-south dynamics, so there exists n>0n>0 such that hk​n​(∂T−(U−∪U+))⊂U−∪U+h^{kn}(\partial T-(U^{-}\cup U^{+}))\subset U^{-}\cup U^{+} for all k≠0k\neq 0. We can therefore apply the ping-pong lemma (see e.g. [35, II.B.24]) to conclude. ∎

Lemma 3.10 (loxodromic-loxodromic, bounded case).

Let TT be a real tree and let GG be a group acting on TT by isometries. Let g,h∈Gg,h\in G be elements acting loxodromically on TT. If Axis⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)\operatorname{Axis}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h) is bounded (possibly empty), then there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2}.

Proof.

This is a direct consequence of, for instance, [31, Lemma 2.6]. ∎

Lemma 3.11 (loxodromic-loxodromic, unbounded case).

Let TT be a real tree and let GG act on TT by isometries. If g,h∈Gg,h\in G both act loxodromically on TT and Axis⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)\operatorname{Axis}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h) is unbounded, then gg and hh fix a common point in ∂T\partial T.

Proof.

This is immediate. ∎

Lemma 3.12 (mixed, unbounded case).

Let TT be a real tree and let GG act on TT under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1. If g,h∈Gg,h\in G, with gg acting elliptically on TT and hh acting loxodromically on TT, and with Fix∞⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h) unbounded, then there exists n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that gng^{n} and hh fix a common point in ∂T\partial T.

Proof.

The stabilisation property applied to the sequence of geodesics {(⋃i=1kFix⁡(gi))∩Axis⁡(h)}n\{(\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\operatorname{Fix}(g^{i}))\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h)\}_{n} implies that there exists an integer kk such that

(⋃i=1kFix⁡(gi))∩Axis⁡(h)=Fix∞⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)(\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\operatorname{Fix}(g^{i}))\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h)=\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h)

Since ⋃i=1kFix⁡(gi)⊂Fix⁡(gk!)\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\operatorname{Fix}(g^{i})\subset\operatorname{Fix}(g^{k!}), we get in particular that Fix⁡(gk!)∩Axis⁡(h)=Fix∞⁡(g)∩Axis⁡(h)\operatorname{Fix}(g^{k!})\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h)=\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Axis}(h). Since this intersection is unbounded by assumption, it follows that gk!g^{k!} and hh fixes a point in ∂T\partial T. Thus, gk!g^{k!} and hh belong to the stabiliser of a common boundary point. ∎

Combining the lemmas gives:

Proposition 3.13.

Let GG act by isometries on the real tree TT and suppose that the action satisfies stabilisation. For all g,h∈Gg,h\in G, there exists n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that either ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2}, or there exists x∈T∪∂Tx\in T\cup\partial T such that gn,hn∈StabG⁡(x)g^{n},h^{n}\in\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x).

Proof.

Each of gg and hh is either elliptic or loxodromic [31, 1.3]. By Lemmas 3.12, 3.11, 3.10, and 3.9, if hh is loxodromic, then either ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2} for suitable nn, or gng^{n} and hnh^{n} stabilise a common point in ∂T\partial T. Otherwise we can conclude using Lemma 3.7. ∎

Theorem 3.1 is now a direct consequence of Proposition 3.13.

4. Examples and first application

We collect here some first direct applications of Theorem 3.1, together with examples and non-examples of groups that satisfy the power alternative. In the last part of the section we will turn our focus on Artin groups that admit a visual splitting, as a more detailed example.

4.1. First applications

To illustrate a typical case of Theorem 3.1, we have the following statement about acylindrical actions on trees (we refer the reader to Definition 6.1 for the definition of acylindricity).

Corollary 4.1.

Let TT be a real tree and let GG act on TT acylindrically. If stabilisers of points of TT satisfy the power alternative, then so does GG.

Proof.

By [56, Theorem 1.1], stabilisers of points in ∂T\partial T either stabilise points of TT or are virtually ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and in particular satisfy the power alternative. Since the action satisfies the stabilisation property by Example 3.5, Theorem 3.1 applies. ∎

In fact, the lemmas used to prove Theorem 3.1 actually give a more general statement without further work; the statement requires a preliminary definition.

Recall what it means for a group GG to satisfy a law. Let F⁡(a1,…,ar)F(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}) be a free group on the generators a1,…,ara_{1},\ldots,a_{r} and let w∈F⁡(a1,…,ar)w\in F(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}) be a nontrivial reduced word. Define a map w:Gr→Gw:G^{r}\to G as follows: given g1,…,gr∈Gg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in G, let w⁡(g1,…,gr)w(g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}) be the image of ww under the homomorphism Fr→GF_{r}\to G induced by ai↦gia_{i}\mapsto g_{i} for i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}. Then GG satisfies the law ww if w⁡(g1,…,gr)=1w(g_{1},\ldots,g_{r})=1 for all g1,…,gr∈Gg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in G.

Definition 4.2 (law-power alternative).

Given w∈Fr−{1}w\in F_{r}-\{1\}, the group GG satisfies the ww–law-power alternative if, for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G, there exists n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that either ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2} or ⟨gn,hn⟩G\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G} satisfies the law ww.

Remark 4.3.

The power alternative is the ww–law-power alternative for w=[a1,a2]∈F⁡(a1,a2)w=[a_{1},a_{2}]\in F(a_{1},a_{2}). One can define uniform versions of the ww–law-power alternative, in analogy to Definition 2.1.

Corollary 4.4.

Fix w∈Fr−{1}w\in F_{r}-\{1\}. Suppose GG acts on the real tree TT satisfying stabilisation and that StabG⁡(x)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x) satisfies the ww–law-power alternative for all x∈T∪∂Tx\in T\cup\partial T. Then GG satisfies the ww–law-power alternative.

Proof.

This follows from Proposition 3.13 and Definition 4.2 along with our assumption on stabilisers. ∎

Before our remaining applications, we need to recall the structure of stabilisers of boundary points.

4.2. Ultimate translation length

Let us introduce the concept of ultimate translation length for an isometry of the real tree TT fixing a point at infinity.

Definition 4.5 (ultimate translation length).

Let TT be a real tree and let GG be a group acting on TT by isometries; the ultimate translation length of g∈StabG⁡(ξ)g\in\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\xi) towards ξ\xi is defined as

utl⁡(g)={τ⁡(g)if g acts loxodromically on T and ξ=g+∞0if g acts elliptically on T−τ⁡(g)if g acts loxodromically on T and ξ=g−∞\operatorname{utl}(g)=\begin{cases}\tau(g)&\text{if~$g$ acts loxodromically on~$T$ and~$\xi=g^{+\infty}$}\\ 0&\text{if~$g$ acts elliptically on~$T$}\\ -\tau(g)&\text{if~$g$ acts loxodromically on~$T$ and~$\xi=g^{-\infty}$}\end{cases}
Lemma 4.6 ([31, Corollary 2.3]).

Let TT be a real tree, let GG be a group acting on TT by isometries and let ξ∈∂T\xi\in\partial T. The function

utlξ:StabG⁡(ξ)\displaystyle\operatorname{utl}_{\xi}\colon\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\xi) →ℝ\displaystyle\to\mathbb{R}
g\displaystyle g ↦utl⁡(g)\displaystyle\mapsto\operatorname{utl}(g)

defines a group homomorphism. If TT is simplicial, then the image of utlξ\operatorname{utl}_{\xi} is in ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Note that an element of StabG⁡(ξ)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\xi) has zero ultimate translation length towards the point at infinity ξ\xi if and only if it fixes pointwise a geodesic ray converging to ξ\xi. Therefore

Ker⁡(utlξ)=∪{StabGpt⁡(γ):γ geodesic ray in T converging to ξ}.\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{utl}_{\xi})=\cup\big\{\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{G}(\gamma):\text{$\gamma$ geodesic ray in~$T$ converging to~$\xi$}\big\}.
Lemma 4.7.

Let TT be a real tree and let GG be a group acting on TT by isometries. Let {In}n∈ℕ\{I_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of geodesic rays converging to ξ\xi such that:

  1. (1)

    for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, In+1⊊InI_{n+1}\subsetneq I_{n};

  2. (2)

    ⋂n∈ℕIn=∅\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}I_{n}=\varnothing;

Then Ker⁡(utlξ)=⋃n∈ℕStabGpt⁡(In)\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{utl}_{\xi})=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{G}(I_{n}).

Proof.

Because {In}n∈ℕ\{I_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is a family of geodesic rays converging to ξ\xi, the inclusion

⋃n∈ℕStabGpt⁡(In)⊂Ker⁡(utlξ)\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{G}(I_{n})\subset\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{utl}_{\xi})

is straightforward. For the reverse inclusion, let g∈Ker⁡(utlξ)g\in\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{utl}_{\xi}), so that there exists a geodesic ray γ⊂T\gamma\subset T converging to ξ\xi, which gg fixes pointwise. Because the sequence of the InI_{n}’s is inclusion-wise decreasing and satisfies ⋂n∈ℕIn=∅\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}I_{n}=\varnothing, there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that In⊂γI_{n}\subset\gamma. ∎

4.3. Combination theorem, examples, and non-examples

The next statement will be used in conjunction with results in Section 6 about mapping tori.

Corollary 4.8.

Let w∈Fr−{1}w\in F_{r}-\{1\}. Suppose GG acts by graph automorphisms, without inversions, on the simplicial tree TT and the action satisfies stabilisation. Let ℭ\mathfrak{C} be the class of exactly those C≤GC\leq G such that C∈ℭC\in\mathfrak{C} is the intersection of finitely many vertex stabilisers. For every z∈Gz\in G and C∈ℭC\in\mathfrak{C} such that C​⊴​⟨C,z⟩G=:HC\trianglelefteq\langle C,z\rangle_{G}=:H, suppose that HH satisfies the ww–law-power alternative. Then GG satisfies the ww–law-power alternative.

Proof.

Let g,h∈Gg,h\in G. By Proposition 3.13, either ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2} for some n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}, or nn can be chosen so that gn,hn∈StabG⁡(x)g^{n},h^{n}\in\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x) for some x∈T∪∂Tx\in T\cup\partial T. If x∈Tx\in T, then our hypothesis on stabilisers applies. Therefore suppose that x∈∂Tx\in\partial T. Consider the homomorphism utlx:StabG⁡(x)→ℤ\operatorname{utl}_{x}\colon\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x)\to\mathbb{Z} from Lemma 4.6. If utl⁡(gn)=utl⁡(hn)=0\operatorname{utl}(g^{n})=\operatorname{utl}(h^{n})=0, then gn,hng^{n},h^{n} stabilise a common point in TT, and we are done. So we may assume that utlx\operatorname{utl}_{x} has nontrivial image in ℤ\mathbb{Z}. By Lemma 4.7 and stabilisation, C=Ker⁡(utlx)∈ℭC=\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{utl}_{x})\in\mathfrak{C}, so we have a short exact sequence 1→C↪StabG⁡(x)↠ℤ→11\rightarrow C\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x)\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow 1. Hence StabG⁡(x)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(x) satisfies the ww–law-power alternative, as required. ∎

As a sample application, we have:

Corollary 4.9.

Let GG split as a finite graph of groups where:

  • •

    Each vertex group GvG_{v} is of one of the following types: GvG_{v} is free; GvG_{v} is the fundamental group of a closed hyperbolic surface; GvG_{v} is a one-ended hyperbolic group with Out⁡(Gv)\operatorname{Out}(G_{v}) finite.

  • •

    Each edge group GeG_{e} is free or a surface group, and quasiconvex in the incident vertex groups.

  • •

    The action of GG on the Bass-Serre tree satisfies stabilisation.

Then GG satisfies the power alternative.

Proof.

Let ℭ0\mathfrak{C}_{0} be the set of subgroups StabG⁡(v)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(v) for v∈Vert⁡(T)v\in\operatorname{Vert}(T). Let ℭ\mathfrak{C} be the set of subgroups of GG arising as finite intersections of elements of ℭ0\mathfrak{C}_{0}. Let C1,…,Cn∈ℭ0C_{1},\ldots,C_{n}\in\mathfrak{C}_{0} and let viv_{i} be a vertex of TT with StabG⁡(vi)=Ci\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(v_{i})=C_{i}.

Let C=⋂i=1nCiC=\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}C_{i}. We claim that CC is hyperbolic. Indeed, if n=1n=1, this holds by hypothesis; in this case it is immediate that C=CnC=C_{n} is quasiconvex in CnC_{n}.

Assume by induction that for all J⊊{1,…,n}J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}, the subgroup CJ=⋂i∈JCiC^{J}=\bigcap_{i\in J}C_{i} is quasiconvex in CiC_{i} for all i∈Ji\in J. Let T′⊂TT^{\prime}\subset T be the finite tree which is the convex hull of {v1,…,vn}\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\}. By relabelling, we can assume vnv_{n} is a leaf of T′T^{\prime}. Let T′′T^{\prime\prime} be the convex hull of {v1,…,vn−1}\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n-1}\}. Let e1,e2,…,eke_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{k} be the sequence of consecutive edges in a shortest path in T′T^{\prime} from vnv_{n} to an arbitrary vertex in {v1,…,vn−1}\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n-1}\}, which we may assume is vn−1v_{n-1}. Let C′=C{v1,…,vn−1}C^{\prime}=C^{\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n-1}\}}. So, by the induction hypothesis, C′C^{\prime} is quasiconvex in Cn−1C_{n-1} (and hence hyperbolic). Now, C=C′∩⋂j=1kStabG⁡(ej)C=C^{\prime}\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^{k}\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(e_{j}). Since edge-groups are intersections of their incident vertex groups, are quasiconvex in those vertex groups by assumption, and since finite intersections of quasiconvex subgroups of a hyperbolic group are quasiconvex, it follows that CC is quasiconvex in CnC_{n}. In particular, each C∈ℭC\in\mathfrak{C} is hyperbolic. By Theorem 6.5 below (which is a well-known fact about hyperbolic groups; see e.g. [53]), each C∈ℭC\in\mathfrak{C} satisfies Wise’s power alternative.

Now let C∈ℭ0C\in\mathfrak{C}_{0} and let H=⟨C,z⟩GH=\langle C,z\rangle_{G} where z∈Gz\in G normalises CC. So, HH is the mapping torus of some automorphism of CC. If CC is the intersection of at least two vertex groups, our hypotheses ensure it is free or a surface group, so either Corollary 6.20 or Corollary 6.18 implies the power alternative for HH. Otherwise, CC is a vertex group, so either the same argument applies, or Out⁡(C)\operatorname{Out}(C) is finite. In the latter case, HH is virtually a direct product of ℤ\mathbb{Z} with a finite-index subgroup of CC, so Lemma 2.2 and Lemma 2.4 imply that HH satisfies the power alternative. Now the result follows from Corollary 4.8. ∎

Remark 4.10.

Corollary 4.9 is intended mainly to illustrate the technical conditions in Corollary 4.8, so we have probably not given the strongest possible statement. Specifically, one can probably allow more general vertex and edge groups, at the expense of complicating the proof in a tangential way. Indeed, if C∈ℭC\in\mathfrak{C} is allowed to be a hyperbolic group that is not free or a surface group, then one can presumably consider first the Grushko decomposition of CC, and then a JSJ decomposition of each one-ended vertex group, to analyse the subgroup ⟨C,z⟩G≅C⋊ℤ\langle C,z\rangle_{G}\cong C\rtimes\mathbb{Z}. In other words, one can likely make a stronger statement if equipped with a generalisation of Corollary 6.18 and Corollary 6.20 for hyperbolic-by-cyclic groups.

Now we turn to negative examples, all involving commensuration of edge groups in one way or another.

Example 4.11.

Let GG be the Baumslag-Solitar group BS⁡(1,n)\operatorname{BS}(1,n). The action of GG on the Bass-Serre tree TT of the usual splitting as an ascending HNN extension of ℤ\mathbb{Z} fixes a point in ∂T\partial T, so any statement, like Theorem 3.1, that assumes the power alternative for stabilisers of boundary points cannot give useful information. And in fact GG does not satisfy the power alternative when |n|>1|n|>1, since [G,G][G,G] is isomorphic to the additive group of nn–adic rationals and hence satisfies the law [[a,b],[c,d]]=1[[a,b],[c,d]]=1 over F4F_{4}.

Example 4.12.

Suppose that GG is a finite graph of groups whose vertex groups are finite-rank free abelian groups and whose edge groups have finite index in the incident vertex groups. Groups of this type with many interesting properties were constructed by Leary-Minasyan in [51].

For such GG, the Bass-Serre tree TT is locally finite and GG acts on TT cocompactly. Let ℭ\mathfrak{C} be the class of finite-rank free abelian subgroups of GG. Obviously ℭ\mathfrak{C} is closed under intersections and elements of CC trivially satisfy the power alternative.

We consider the specific example G=Gk,mG=G_{k,m} from [51, Example 9.4], with −2​m<k<2​m-2m<k<2m and k∉{0,±m}k\not\in\{0,\pm m\}. Such a GG does not satisfy the power alternative, by [51, Corollary 9.6].

Then by [51, Corollary 9.3], GG is a CAT⁡(0)\operatorname{CAT}(0) group, and in fact, by [51, Theorem 7.2 and Theorem 7.5], GG is a uniform lattice in 𝔼2×T\mathbb{E}^{2}\times T. In particular, the vertex and edge stabilisers for the action on TT are in ℭ\mathfrak{C}. However, the stabilisation property fails in this case.

Example 4.13.

Let T1,T2T_{1},T_{2} be locally finite trees and suppose that G≤Isom⁡(T1)×Isom⁡(T2)G\leq\operatorname{Isom}(T_{1})\times\operatorname{Isom}(T_{2}) is a cocompact irreducible lattice as in [26][67]. Then the vertex stabilisers and edge-stabilisers are finite-rank free groups; let ℭ\mathfrak{C} be the class of finite-rank free groups in GG that are elliptic on T1T_{1}. Then ℭ\mathfrak{C} is closed under finite intersections (the stabiliser of any point in T1T_{1} is a commensurated subgroup of GG). Irreducibility means that the image of GG in Isom⁡(T1)\operatorname{Isom}(T_{1}) is non-discrete [27, Theorem 1.4]. It is an open question when such T1×T2T_{1}\times T_{2} must contain an anti-torus, i.e. an isometrically embedded flat FF such that the map F↪T1×T2→(T1×T2)/GF\hookrightarrow T_{1}\times T_{2}\to(T_{1}\times T_{2})/G does not factor through a π1\pi_{1}–injective torus, but FF is the convex hull in T1×T2T_{1}\times T_{2} of a pair of axes of elements a1,a2a_{1},a_{2}, with aia_{i} acting hyperbolically on TiT_{i} (and elliptically on the other tree). The projection of an anti-torus to one of the TiT_{i} contains a ray witnessing the failure of the stabilisation property. And the subgroup ⟨a1,a2⟩\langle a_{1},a_{2}\rangle has the property that nontrivial powers of a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} do not commute. But it is unknown if GG satisfies the power alternative even in the absence of stabilisation.

4.4. Artin groups and visual splittings

We devote the remaining part of the section to prove a sufficient condition determining when an Artin group with a visual splitting satisfies the power alternative.

Definition 4.14 (Artin groups).

Let Γ=(Vert⁡(Γ),Edge⁡(Γ))\Gamma=(\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma),\operatorname{Edge}(\Gamma)) be a finite simplicial graph;

  1. (1)

    A labelling of Γ\Gamma is a map m:Edge⁡(Γ)→ℕ≥2m\colon\operatorname{Edge}(\Gamma)\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}. If {s,t}\{s,t\} is an edge of Γ\Gamma, then we write ms​tm_{st} in place of m⁡({s,t})m(\{s,t\}). We call the pair (Γ,m)(\Gamma,m) a presentation graph;

  2. (2)

    Let (Γ,m)(\Gamma,m) be a presentation graph; the Artin group associated to (Γ,m)(\Gamma,m) is the group AΓA_{\Gamma} with presentation

    ⟨Vert(Γ)∣sts⋯⏟ms​t=tst⋯⏟ms​t for all {s,t}∈Edge⁡(Γ)⟩\langle\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma)\mid\underbrace{sts\cdots}_{m_{st}}=\underbrace{tst\cdots}_{m_{st}}\text{ for all $\{s,t\}\in\operatorname{Edge}(\Gamma)$}\rangle
  3. (3)

    the Coxeter group associated to Γ\Gamma is the quotient WΓW_{\Gamma} of AΓA_{\Gamma} by the normal closure of the subgroup generated by {s2:s∈Vert⁡(Γ)}\{s^{2}:s\in\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma)\}.

We will often “forget” about the labelling and refer to AΓA_{\Gamma} as the Artin group associated to Γ\Gamma.

If Γ\Gamma is a graph and Λ≤Γ\Lambda\leq\Gamma is a subgraph, recall that Λ\Lambda is said to be the full subgraph of Γ\Gamma induced by Vert⁡(Λ)\operatorname{Vert}(\Lambda) (or just a full subgraph) if every edge of Γ\Gamma connecting two vertices of Λ\Lambda is also an edge of Λ\Lambda.

For every subset SS of vertices of Γ\Gamma we can consider the subgroup ⟨S⟩AΓ\langle S\rangle_{A_{\Gamma}} of AΓA_{\Gamma} generated by SS. Such a subgroup is called the standard parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} generated by SS and is denoted ASA_{S}. If ΓS\Gamma_{S} denotes the full subgraph of Γ\Gamma spanned by SS, then ASA_{S} is isomorphic to AΓSA_{\Gamma_{S}} b y a result of van der Lek [66]. A subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} that is conjugated to a standard parabolic subgroup is called a parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}. The inclusion between parabolic subgroups is well-understood.

Theorem 4.15 (inclusion of parabolic subgroups, [21]*Theorem 1.1).

Let Γ\Gamma be a finite labelled simplicial graph and let X,Y⊂Vert⁡(Γ)X,Y\subset\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma). If g​AX​g−1≤AYgA_{X}g^{-1}\leq A_{Y} for some g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma}, then there exist Z⊂YZ\subset Y and h∈AYh\in A_{Y} such that g​AX​g−1=h​AZ​h−1gA_{X}g^{-1}=hA_{Z}h^{-1}.

In particular, if g​AX​g−1<AYgA_{X}g^{-1}<A_{Y}, then |X|<|Y||X|<|Y|.

Group-theoretic results holding for all Artin groups are quite rare and it is common to restrict to certain families of such groups instead. We recall here the definition of the most common ones.

Definition 4.16 (families of Artin groups).

Let Γ\Gamma be a finite presentation graph. We say that the associated Artin group AΓA_{\Gamma} is:

  1. (1)

    dihedral if |Vert⁡(Γ)|=2\lvert\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma)\rvert=2;

  2. (2)

    two-dimensional if, for every r,s,tr,s,t distinct vertices of Γ\Gamma,

    1mr​s+1ms​t+1mt​r≤1\frac{1}{m_{rs}}+\frac{1}{m_{st}}+\frac{1}{m_{tr}}\leq 1

    with the convention that 1/mr​s=01/m_{rs}=0, when {r,s}\{r,s\} is not an edge of Γ\Gamma;

  3. (3)

    spherical if the associated Coxeter group WΓW_{\Gamma} is finite;

  4. (4)

    of hyperbolic-type if the associated Coxeter group WΓW_{\Gamma} is hyperbolic;

  5. (5)

    of FC-type if every clique of Γ\Gamma induces a spherical parabolic subgroup;

  6. (6)

    even if all the labels of Γ\Gamma are even.

Much of our current understanding of Artin groups comes from our understanding of their parabolic subgroups. The following two properties are conjectured to holds for all Artin groups [38]*Conjecture 1.

Definition 4.17 (structure of normalisers, intersection of parabolics).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group.

  1. (1)

    For S⊂Vert⁡(Γ)S\subset\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma) we define the quasi-centraliser of ASA_{S} in AΓA_{\Gamma} as

    QZAΓ⁡(AS)={g∈AΓ:g​S​g−1=S}\operatorname{QZ}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{S})=\{g\in A_{\Gamma}:gSg^{-1}=S\}

    We say that AΓA_{\Gamma} enjoys the normaliser structure property if, for every S⊂Vert⁡(Γ)S\subset\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma), one has

    NAΓ⁡(AS)=AS⋅QZAΓ⁡(AS)\operatorname{N}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{S})=A_{S}\cdot\operatorname{QZ}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{S})
  2. (2)

    We say that AΓA_{\Gamma} has the parabolic intersection property if, for all parabolic subgroups P,Q≤AΓP,Q\leq A_{\Gamma}, the intersection P∩QP\cap Q is a parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}.

Godelle proved the normaliser structure property for Artin groups of FC-type and for two-dimensional Artin groups [37][38]. As for the parabolic intersection property, Blufstein proved it for the family of two-dimensional (2,2)(2,2)-free Artin groups [20] and Antolín and Foniqi proved it for the family of even FC type Artin groups [6].

Visual splittings

For an amalgamated product of two groups there is a natural choice of tree to act on, namely the associated Bass-Serre tree. In the context of Artin groups, certain amalgamated product decompositions can be read directly from the defining graph (see for instance [29]). Let Γ\Gamma be a presentation graph and let Γ0≤Γ1,Γ2<Γ\Gamma_{0}\leq\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}<\Gamma be non-empty induced subgraphs such that Γ1∪Γ2=Γ\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{2}=\Gamma and Γ1∩Γ2=Γ0\Gamma_{1}\cap\Gamma_{2}=\Gamma_{0}. This data gives an isomorphism

AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ2≅AΓA_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{2}}\cong A_{\Gamma}

at the level of the associated Artin groups and the amalgamated product AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{2}} is called a visual splitting for AΓA_{\Gamma}. In this section, we will denote by TT the Bass-Serre tree associated with the amalgamation AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{2}}.

Lemma 4.18.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group satisfying the intersection property. Consider the action AΓ↷TA_{\Gamma}\curvearrowright T on the Bass–Serre tree corresponding to some visual splitting. Then for every geodesic γ\gamma of TT, the pointwise stabiliser of γ\gamma is a parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}.

Proof.

Stabilisers of vertices of TT are parabolic subgroups by definition of a visual splitting. Since the action on TT is without inversion, an element of AΓA_{\Gamma} fixes γ\gamma pointwise if and only if it fixes every vertex of that geodesic, and the result then follows from the intersection property for AΓA_{\Gamma}. ∎

Lemma 4.19.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group satisfying the intersection property. Consider the action AΓ↷TA_{\Gamma}\curvearrowright T on the Bass–Serre tree corresponding to some visual splitting. Then this action has the stabilisation property.

Proof.

Since stabilisers of geodesics are parabolic subgroups by Lemma 4.18, the result follows from the fact that strict chains of parabolic subgroups have bounded length by Theorem 4.15. ∎

Proof of Corollary B

The key result for the proof of Corollary B is the following observation.

Lemma 4.20.

Let AΓ≅AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ2A_{\Gamma}\cong A_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{2}} be an Artin groups expressed as a visual splitting satisfying the hypotheses of Corollary B. Let ℭ\mathfrak{C} be the set of parabolic subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma} that are conjugated with a parabolic subgroup of AΓ1A_{\Gamma_{1}} or AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{2}}. For every z∈AΓz\in A_{\Gamma} and for every P∈ℭP\in\mathfrak{C} such that P​⊴​⟨P,z⟩=:HP\trianglelefteq\langle P,z\rangle=\colon H, either HH is virtually PP or HH contains a finite-index subgroup of the form P×ℤP\times\mathbb{Z}. In particular, HH satisfies the power alternative.

Proof.

Up to a conjugation in AΓA_{\Gamma}, we can assume that PP is a standard parabolic subgroup ASA_{S}, for some S⊂Vert⁡(Γ1)S\subset\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma_{1}) or S⊂Vert⁡(Γ2)S\subset\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma_{2}). Because the power alternative holds for AΓ1A_{\Gamma_{1}} and AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{2}}, every element of ℭ\mathfrak{C} satisfies it. If zz is torsion, then HH is virtually ASA_{S}. We can then assume that zz has infinite order. By assumption, we have that zz normalises ASA_{S}. By the normaliser structure property for AΓA_{\Gamma}, NAΓ⁡(AS)≅AS⋅QZAΓ⁡(AS)\operatorname{N}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{S})\cong A_{S}\cdot\operatorname{QZ}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{S}) and, up to a translation in ASA_{S}, we may assume that z∈QZAΓ⁡(AS)z\in\operatorname{QZ}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{S}). Because SS is a finite set, a non-trivial power znz^{n} centralises ASA_{S}. In particular, HH (which is a semi-direct product of the form AS⋊ℤA_{S}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}) has a finite-index subgroup that is isomorphic to a direct product AS×ℤA_{S}\times\mathbb{Z}. The final claim follows by Lemma 2.4. ∎

We are now ready to prove Corollary B.

Proof of Corollary B.

Let TT be the Bass-Serre tree associated to the visual splitting of AΓA_{\Gamma}. The action satisfies the stabilisation property by Lemma 4.19. Let ℭ\mathfrak{C} be the family of those subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma} that arise as finite intersections of stabilisers of TT, so, in particular, ℭ\mathfrak{C} consists of parabolic subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma} that are conjugated with parabolic subgroups of AΓ1A_{\Gamma_{1}} or AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{2}}. By combining Lemma 4.20 and Corollary 4.8, we obtain the claim. ∎

Remark 4.21.

The approach developed in this section can also be used to recover the power alternative for graph products of groups satisfying the power alternative. Indeed, similarly to Artin groups, there is a well-defined notion of parabolic subgroup and of visual decomposition for these groups. The intersection property for graph products follows from [7, Corollary 3.6], and the structure of the normalizer of a parabolic subgroup follows from [7, Proposition 3.13]. Thus, an application of Corollary 4.8, following a similar proof as above, reduces the power alternative for a given (irreducible) graph product of groups to the power alternative for the various direct products of local groups, and thus to the local groups themselves by Lemma 2.4.

Note that every Artin group can be obtained via a sequence of amalgamated products over standard parabolic subgroups, terminating at Artin groups with complete presentation graphs (also called free-of-infinity Artin groups). In particular, Corollary B implies the following “reduction” theorem, under the hypothesis that the intersection property and the normalizer property hold:

Corollary 4.22.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a class of Artin groups that is closed under taking standard parabolic subgroups and under taking amalagamated products over standard parabolic subgroups. Suppose that the intersection property and the normalizer property hold for all Artin groups in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Then if the power alternative holds for all free-of-infinity Artin groups in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then it holds for all Artin groups in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

5. The uniform power alternative for (2,2)(2,2)-free triangle-free Artin groups

In this section, we show that some Artin groups satisfy the uniform power alternative, with a uniform exponent depending only on the set of labels of the defining graph.

Definition 5.1.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group with presentation graph Γ\Gamma. We say that:

  • •

    AΓA_{\Gamma} is triangle-free if Γ\Gamma does not contain an induced 33-cycle.

  • •

    AΓA_{\Gamma} is (2,2)-free if Γ\Gamma does not contain two adjacent edges with label 22.

Note that triangle-free Artin groups are in particular 22-dimensional Artin groups of FC type. Moreover (2,2)(2,2)-free and triangle-free Artin groups are additionally of hyperbolic type.

Our approach to prove Theorem C is via the following relative notion:

Definition 5.2 (relative uniform power alternative).

Let N∈ℕ≥1N\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}; the Artin group AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the power alternative relative to complete parabolics with uniform exponent NN if, for every g,h∈AΓg,h\in A_{\Gamma}, one of the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    gg and hh belong to a common parabolic subgroup based on a complete subgraph of Γ\Gamma;

  2. (2)

    ⟨gN,hN⟩AΓ\langle g^{N},h^{N}\rangle_{A_{\Gamma}} is either abelian or non-abelian free.

For the sake of conciseness we will refer to the notion of uniform power alternative relative to complete parabolics just as the relative uniform power alternative. The focus of this section will be to prove the relative uniform power alternative for the class of (2,2)(2,2)-free triangle-free Artin groups:

Theorem 5.3 (relative uniform power alternative).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group whose defining graph is (2,2)(2,2)-free and triangle-free. For every N∈ℕ≥3N\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}, AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the relative power alternative with uniform exponent NN.

If the group AΓA_{\Gamma} enjoys the relative power alternative and every standard parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} based on a complete graph satisfies the uniform power alternative, then AΓA_{\Gamma} inherits the uniform power alternative in the following sense:

Lemma 5.4.

Let N0∈ℕ≥1N_{0}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} and let the Artin group AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfy the relative uniform power alternative with uniform exponent NN for every N≥N0N\geq N_{0}. Let us further assume that, for every complete subgraph Λ≤Γ\Lambda\leq\Gamma, there exists mΛ∈ℕ≥1m_{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} such that the group AΛA_{\Lambda} satisfies the power alternative with uniform exponent mΛm_{\Lambda}. We denote by KK the number

K=lcm⁡{mΛ:Λ≤Γ complete subgraph}K=\operatorname{lcm}\left\{m_{\Lambda}:\text{$\Lambda\leq\Gamma$ complete subgraph}\right\}

Then AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the power alternative with uniform exponent

N≔min⁡{α​K:α∈ℕ≥1 and α​K≥N0}N\coloneqq\min\{\alpha K:\text{$\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}$ and $\alpha K\geq N_{0}$}\}
Proof.

Let g,h∈AΓg,h\in A_{\Gamma}. If gg and hh do not belong to a common parabolic subgroup based on a complete subgraph, then since N≥N0N\geq N_{0} by construction and AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the relative uniform power alternative with uniform exponent NN, we have that ⟨gN,hN⟩AΓ\langle g^{N},h^{N}\rangle_{A_{\Gamma}} is either abelian or non-abelian free. If gg and hh belong to the conjugate of some parabolic AΛA_{\Lambda} for some complete subgraph Λ≤Γ\Lambda\leq\Gamma, then NN is a multiple of mΛm_{\Lambda} by construction, and thus gg and hh also satisfy the power alternative with exponent NN. ∎

As a particular case of this theorem, we obtain Corollary C. We first need the following:

Theorem 5.5 ([30]*Section 2).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a spherical dihedral Artin group with label m∈ℕ≥3m\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3} and let us define

m′={m/2if m is even2​mif m is oddm^{\prime}=\begin{cases}m/2&\text{if $m$ is even}\\ 2m&\text{if $m$ is odd}\end{cases}

Then AΓA_{\Gamma} contains a subgroups of index m′m^{\prime} that is isomorphic to ℤ×Fk\mathbb{Z}\times F_{k} for some k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}. In particular, AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the power alternative with uniform exponent m′m^{\prime}.

Proof of Corollary C.

By Theorem 5.3, AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the relative power alternative with uniform exponent NN for every N∈ℕ≥3N\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}. It is sufficient to show that every standard parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} based on a complete graph satisfies the uniform power alternative. Therefore, let Λ≤Γ\Lambda\leq\Gamma be a complete subgraph. Because AΓA_{\Gamma} is two-dimensional, Λ\Lambda has at most two vertices, the only non-trivial case being when Λ\Lambda has exactly two vertices. In such case, Theorem 5.5 yields the claim. ∎

5.1. Further background on Artin groups

We collect here some further background results that are not yet known for general Artin groups but which hold when restricting to the class of two-dimensional Artin groups. Note that triangle-free Artin groups are two-dimensional, in particular. In view of the results discussed in Section 4.4, we have the following theorem.

Theorem 5.6.

If AΓA_{\Gamma} is (2,2)(2,2)-free and triangle-free, then AΓA_{\Gamma} has the intersection property and the normaliser structure property.

Normalisers of parabolic subgroups

As mentioned in Section 4, normalisers of parabolics of two-dimensional Artin groups are well-understood. For the class that we consider in this section, an even stronger result holds.

Theorem 5.7 (normalisers of parabolics, [54]*Lemma 4.5[38]*Corollary 4.12).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a (2,2)(2,2)-free triangle-free Artin group and let Λ≤Γ\Lambda\leq\Gamma be a full subgraph;

  1. (1)

    if Λ\Lambda consists of a single vertex aa, then NAΓ⁡(AΛ)=CAΓ⁡(a)\operatorname{N}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{\Lambda})=\operatorname{C}_{A_{\Gamma}}(a) and, moreover, there exists k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that CAΓ⁡(a)≅ℤ×Fk\operatorname{C}_{A_{\Gamma}}(a)\cong\mathbb{Z}\times F_{k};

  2. (2)

    if |Vert⁡(Λ)|≥2\lvert\operatorname{Vert}(\Lambda)\rvert\geq 2, then NAΓ⁡(AΛ)=AΛ\operatorname{N}_{A_{\Gamma}}(A_{\Lambda})=A_{\Lambda}.

The way to conjugate parabolic subgroups amongst each other is also fully understood for this class of Artin groups, using the key concept of ribbons, which was introduced by Paris [57]. The following theorem, which we will need for the proof of Lemma 5.13, follows as a corollary of the facts that two-dimensional Artin groups satisfy the so-called “ribbon conjecture” [38]*Conjecture 1.

Theorem 5.8 (conjugated parabolics, [38]*Theorem 3).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a two-dimensional Artin group and let X,Y⊂Vert⁡(Γ)X,Y\subset\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma) be subsets of cardinality at least two. If AXA_{X} and AYA_{Y} are conjugated in AΓA_{\Gamma}, then X=YX=Y.

Closure under taking roots

The last property we want to address is the one of having the parabolic subgroups that are closed under taking roots.

Definition 5.9 (closure under taking roots).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group; we say that the parabolic subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma} are closed under taking roots if the following property holds: for every parabolic subgroup P≤AΓP\leq A_{\Gamma}, for every g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} and for every n∈ℕ≥1n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}, if gn∈Pg^{n}\in P, then g∈Pg\in P.

Although this property is not known in general, it holds for the class of Artin groups we are studying in this section:

Theorem 5.10 ([38]*Corollary 3.8).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a two-dimensional Artin group. Then parabolic subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma} are closed under taking roots.

Lemma 5.11.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group whose parabolics are closed under taking roots and let us assume that it is expressed as a visual splitting AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{2}} with associated Bass-Serre tree TT. For every element g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} acting elliptically on TT,

Fix∞⁡(g)=Fix⁡(g).\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)=\operatorname{Fix}(g).

In particular, if g,h∈AΓg,h\in A_{\Gamma} are elements acting elliptically on TT, then either ⟨g,h⟩≅F2\langle g,h\rangle\cong F_{2} or gg and hh belong to a common proper parabolic subgroup.

Proof.

For the first statement, note that stabilisers of fixed-point sets are parabolic subgroups and these are are closed under taking roots by hypothesis. The proof of the second statement goes along the lines of the proof of Lemma 3.7. ∎

5.2. Relative uniform power alternative for (2,2)-free triangle-free groups

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 5.3, namely that (2,2)(2,2)-free triangle-free Artin groups satisfy the relative uniform power alternative. Therefore, let AΓ=AΓ1∗AΓ0AΓ1A_{\Gamma}=A_{\Gamma_{1}}*_{A_{\Gamma_{0}}}A_{\Gamma_{1}} be a triangle-free and (2,2)(2,2)-free Artin group expressed as a visual splitting and let TT be the Bass-Serre tree associated to the splitting. We start with an elementary observation:

Lemma 5.12 (properties of fixed trees).

Let P≤AΓP\leq A_{\Gamma} be a parabolic subgroup.

  1. (1)

    the fixed-point set Fix⁡(P)={x∈T:P⋅x=x}\operatorname{Fix}(P)=\{x\in T:P\cdot x=x\} is a subtree of TT;

  2. (2)

    for every g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma}, g⋅Fix⁡(P)=Fix⁡(g​P​g−1)g\cdot\operatorname{Fix}(P)=\operatorname{Fix}(gPg^{-1});

We call Fix⁡(P)\operatorname{Fix}(P) the fixed tree associated to the parabolic subgroup PP.

Lemma 5.13.

Let γ⊂T\gamma\subset T be a geodesic segment that contains at least two edges of TT. If StabAΓpt⁡(γ)\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(\gamma) is an infinite group, then it is an infinite cyclic parabolic subgroup, and γ\gamma is contained in a fixed tree Fix⁡(a)\operatorname{Fix}(a), for some a∈Vert⁡(Γ)a\in\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma).

Proof.

Because the parabolic intersection property holds for AΓA_{\Gamma}, StabAΓpt⁡(γ)\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(\gamma) is a parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} [20]*Theorem 1.3. Let us distinguish two cases, depending on the rank of StabAΓpt⁡(γ)\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(\gamma).

If StabAΓpt⁡(γ)\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(\gamma) is cyclic, then it is of the form g​⟨a⟩​g−1g\langle a\rangle g^{-1} for some g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} and some a∈Vert⁡(Γ0)a\in\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma_{0}). In this case, γ\gamma is contained in the fixed tree g⋅Fix⁡(a)g\cdot\operatorname{Fix}(a).

Let us assume by contradiction that P=StabAΓpt⁡(γ)P=\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(\gamma) is a parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} of rank at least two. Let e={AΓ1,AΓ2}e=\{A_{\Gamma_{1}},A_{\Gamma_{2}}\} be the canonical fundamental domain for the action AΓ↷TA_{\Gamma}\curvearrowright T. Up to a translation in TT, we may assume that γ\gamma contains ee. As AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{2}} acts transitively on the edges around the vertex of ee corresponding to the coset of AΓ2A_{\Gamma_{2}}, let h∈AΓ2∖AΓ0h\in A_{\Gamma_{2}}\smallsetminus A_{\Gamma_{0}} be such that γ\gamma contains the concatenation e∪h⋅ee\cup h\cdot e. Because PP fixes ee pointwise, we obtain that P≤StabAΓpt⁡(e)=AΓ0P\leq\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(e)=A_{\Gamma_{0}}. Thus, by Theorem 4.15, PP is of the form P=g−1​AΛ​gP=g^{-1}A_{\Lambda}g for some g∈AΓ0g\in A_{\Gamma_{0}} and some Λ≤Γ0\Lambda\leq\Gamma_{0}. Because PP also fixes h⋅eh\cdot e pointwise, we obtain that P≤StabAΓpt⁡(h⋅e)=h​AΓ0​h−1P\leq\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(h\cdot e)=hA_{\Gamma_{0}}h^{-1} or, equivalently, h−1​P​h≤AΓ0h^{-1}Ph\leq A_{\Gamma_{0}}. Again, by Theorem 4.15 there are M≤Γ0M\leq\Gamma_{0} and k∈AΓ0k\in A_{\Gamma_{0}} such that h−1​P​h=k​AM​k−1h^{-1}Ph=kA_{M}k^{-1} or, equivalently, (h​k)​AM​(h​k)−1=P(hk)A_{M}(hk)^{-1}=P. In particular, the element g​h​kghk conjugates AΛA_{\Lambda} and AMA_{M} in AΓA_{\Gamma}. Since AΓA_{\Gamma} is two-dimensional and Λ\Lambda contains at least two vertices, it follows from Theorem 5.8 that Λ=M\Lambda=M, hence g​h​kghk normalises AΛA_{\Lambda}. It now follows from Theorem 5.7 that g​h​kghk belongs to AΛA_{\Lambda} itself, giving that h∈AΓ0h\in A_{\Gamma_{0}}, in particular, hence h⋅e=eh\cdot e=e, a contradiction. ∎

Corollary 5.14.

If AΛA_{\Lambda} is a parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma} on more than one vertex, then the fixed-point set of AΛA_{\Lambda} in TT is either empty, a single vertex, or a single edge.

Let us now study the different possible dynamics of pairs of elements of AΓA_{\Gamma} on the Bass-Serre tree TT.

Lemma 5.15.

Let g,h∈AΓg,h\in A_{\Gamma} be two elements with gg acting loxodromically on TT with translation length τ⁡(g)\tau(g). If the intersection Axis⁡(g)∩Min⁡(h)\mathrm{Axis}(g)\cap\operatorname{Min}(h) has length at least 2​max⁡{τ⁡(g),τ⁡(h)}+22\max\{\tau(g),\tau(h)\}+2 (with the usual convention that τ⁡(h)=0\tau(h)=0 if hh acts elliptically), then Axis⁡(g)⊂Min⁡(h)\mathrm{Axis}(g)\subset\operatorname{Min}(h).

Proof.

Let Λ≔Axis⁡(g)∩Min⁡(h)\Lambda\coloneqq\mathrm{Axis}(g)\cap\operatorname{Min}(h), and suppose that this overlap has length at least 2​max⁡{τ⁡(g),τ⁡(h)}+22\max\{\tau(g),\tau(h)\}+2. Let Λ′⊂Λ\Lambda^{\prime}\subset\Lambda be an initial subsegment of Λ\Lambda of length 22. Up to replacing gg by g−1g^{-1}, we can assume that gg and hh translate in the same direction along Λ\Lambda, and we get h​g​Λ′=g​h​Λ′hg\Lambda^{\prime}=gh\Lambda^{\prime}. In particular, the commutator [g,h][g,h] fixes pointwise Λ′\Lambda^{\prime}. By Lemma 5.13, there exists a conjugate ss of a standard generator, and an integer nn such that [g,h]=sn[g,h]=s^{n}. By applying the height homomorphism AΓ→ℤA_{\Gamma}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z} that maps every standard generator to 11, we get that n=0n=0, hence gg and hh commute. In particular, gg preserves Min⁡(h)\operatorname{Min}(h). Since gg acts loxodromically by hypothesis, it follows that Axis⁡(g)⊂Min⁡(h)\mathrm{Axis}(g)\subset\operatorname{Min}(h). ∎

Corollary 5.16.

Let g,h∈AΓg,h\in A_{\Gamma} be two elements with gg acting loxodromically on TT. One of the following two conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    the elements gg and hh belong to a common proper parabolic subgroup;

  2. (2)

    for every n≥3n\geq 3, ⟨gn,hn⟩AΓ\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{A_{\Gamma}} is either abelian free or non-abelian free.

Proof.

Let Λ≔Axis⁡(g)∩Min⁡(h)\Lambda\coloneqq\mathrm{Axis}(g)\cap\mathrm{Min}(h). We consider two cases, depending on the size of this overlap. In the case of hh acting loxodromically as well, it is not restrictive to assume that τ⁡(g)≥τ⁡(h)\tau(g)\geq\tau(h).

First assume that |Λ|<2​max⁡{τ⁡(g),τ⁡(h)}+2=2​τ​(g)+2\lvert\Lambda\rvert<2\max\{\tau(g),\tau(h)\}+2=2\tau(g)+2. Since the translation length of gg on TT is even, it follows that, for every k≥3k\geq 3, the segments gk​Λg^{k}\Lambda and Λ\Lambda are disjoint. It now follows from a standard ping-pong argument that gkg^{k} and hh (and hence gkg^{k} and hkh^{k}) generate a free subgroup.

If |Λ|≥2​τ​(g)+2\lvert\Lambda\rvert\geq 2\tau(g)+2, then it follows from Lemma 5.15 that Axis⁡(g)⊂Min⁡(h)\mathrm{Axis}(g)\subset\operatorname{Min}(h). In particular, gg and hh normalise P≔StabAΓpt⁡(Λ)P\coloneqq\operatorname{Stab}^{\operatorname{pt}}_{A_{\Gamma}}(\Lambda). Since AΓA_{\Gamma} satisfies the Intersection Property, it follows that PP is a parabolic subgroup. There are thus two cases to consider: if PP is a cyclic parabolic subgroup, then its normaliser is of the form ℤ×Fk\mathbb{Z}\times F_{k} by the first case of Theorem 5.7, so gg and hh (hence their powers) either commute or generate a non-abelian free subgroup. If PP is a parabolic subgroup on at least two generators, then PP is self-normalising by Theorem 5.7, point two. Thus, gg and hh are contained in NAΓ⁡(P)=P\operatorname{N}_{A_{\Gamma}}(P)=P, which is a proper parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}, as it is contained in some edge stabiliser. ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 5.3:

Proof of Theorem 5.3.

We prove the result by induction on the number of generators. The initialisation case is the case of dihedral Artin groups and this follows from Theorem 5.5.

Let us now assume that the result has been proved for graphs on less than n≥2n\geq 2 vertices, and let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group with a presentation graph Γ\Gamma on n+1≥3n+1\geq 3 vertices, satisfying the assumption of the theorem. Since AΓA_{\Gamma} is triangle-free on at least three vertices, it follows that Γ\Gamma is not a complete graph, hence we can consider a visual splitting of AΓA_{\Gamma}, and the action of AΓA_{\Gamma} on the corresponding Bass–Serre tree TT. Let g,hg,h be two elements of AΓA_{\Gamma}. There are two cases to consider:

  • •

    if at least one between gg and hh acts loxodromically on TT, it follows from Corollary 5.16 that either gg and hh belong to a common proper parabolic subgroup or, for every k≥3k\geq 3, ⟨gk,hk⟩AΓ≅F2\langle g^{k},h^{k}\rangle_{A_{\Gamma}}\cong F_{2};

  • •

    if gg and hh both act elliptically, then the second part of Lemma 5.11 gives the claim.

In both cases, either for every k≥3k\geq 3, gkg^{k} and hkh^{k} generate a non-abelian free subgroup, or gg and hh belong to a common proper parabolic subgroup on at most nn generators. The result now follows from the induction hypothesis. ∎

5.3. Application: Uniform exponential growth

In this subsection, we use previous results on the uniform power alternative to obtain a strong form of uniform exponential growth for certain Artin groups:

Theorem 5.17.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a triangle-free (2,2)(2,2)-free Artin group that is not of spherical type. Let mm be the smallest multiple of lcma​b∈Edge⁡(Γ)​(ma​b′)\mathrm{lcm}_{ab\in\operatorname{Edge}(\Gamma)}(m_{ab}^{\prime}) such that m≥3m\geq 3, where the coefficients ma​b′m_{ab}^{\prime} were defined in Theorem 5.5.

Let SS be a generating set of AΓA_{\Gamma}. Then there exist s,t∈Ss,t\in S such that sms^{m} and tmt^{m} generate a non-abelian free subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}. In particular, AΓA_{\Gamma} has uniform exponential growth.

The proof of this theorem relies on the action of these Artin groups on their Deligne complex. We recall the definition of these complexes, with both their simplicial and cubical structure.

Definition 5.18 (simplicial and cubical Deligne complex [28]).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be an Artin group. The (simplicial) Deligne complex is the following simplicial complex:

  • •

    vertices of DΓD_{\Gamma} correspond to left cosets g​AΓ′gA_{\Gamma^{\prime}} of spherical standard parabolic subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma};

  • •

    simplices correspond to chains g​AΓ0⊊⋯⊊g​AΓkgA_{\Gamma_{0}}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq gA_{\Gamma_{k}}, for g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} and Γ0⊊⋯⊊Γk⊂Γ\Gamma_{0}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\Gamma_{k}\subset\Gamma such that each AΓiA_{\Gamma_{i}} is spherical.

The cubical Deligne complex CΓC_{\Gamma} is the cube complex with the same vertex set as DΓD_{\Gamma}, and where cubes correspond to combinatorial intervals (for the inclusion) between vertices of CΓC_{\Gamma} of the form g​AΓ0gA_{\Gamma_{0}} and g​AΓkgA_{\Gamma_{k}}, whenever g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} and Γ0⊊Γk\Gamma_{0}\subsetneq\Gamma_{k}.

The group AΓA_{\Gamma} acts on CΓC_{\Gamma} and on DΓD_{\Gamma} by left multiplication on left cosets. These actions are without inversions: An element of AΓA_{\Gamma} stabilises a cube of CΓC_{\Gamma} (resp. a simplex of DΓD_{\Gamma}) if and only if it fixes it pointwise.

The geometry of Deligne complexes is well understood for two-dimensional Artin groups and for FC-type Artin groups, among other classes. Triangle-free Artin groups are in particular two-dimensional and FC-type Artin groups. Moreover, triangle-free Artin groups that are (2,2)(2,2)-free are also of hyperbolic type. We therefore have the following results:

Theorem 5.19 ([28]*Theorem 4.3.5).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a triangle-free Artin group. Then the cubical Deligne complex CΓC_{\Gamma} is a CAT⁡(0)\operatorname{CAT}(0) cube complex.

Theorem 5.20 ([28]*Proposition 4.4.5[54]*Section 3.1).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a triangle-free Artin group. Then the simplicial Deligne complex DΓD_{\Gamma} admits a CAT⁡(0)\operatorname{CAT}(0) metric. Moreover, if AΓA_{\Gamma} is (2,2)(2,2)-free, then AΓA_{\Gamma} is of hyperbolic type, and DΓD_{\Gamma} admits a CAT⁡(−1)\operatorname{CAT}(-1) metric.

Note that one can obtain the simplicial Deligne complex by subdividing in a suitable way the cubes of the corresponding cubical Deligne complex. Thus, the results about the action of AΓA_{\Gamma} on DΓD_{\Gamma}, and in particular the description of the minsets and fixed-point sets in DΓD_{\Gamma} obtained in [54], carry over to the cubical setting without any change:

Lemma 5.21 ([54]).

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a triangle-free Artin group. Let g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} be an element acting elliptically on the cubical Deligne complex CΓC_{\Gamma}.

  • •

    If gg is conjugated to a power of a standard generator, then the fixed-point set of gg is a tree contained in the 11-skeleton of CΓC_{\Gamma}, called a standard tree.

  • •

    Otherwise, the fixed-point set of gg is a single vertex of CΓC_{\Gamma}, whose stabiliser is conjugated to a dihedral standard parabolic subgroup of AΓA_{\Gamma}.

Lemma 5.22.

Let AΓA_{\Gamma} be a triangle-free Artin group. Let g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma} be an element acting elliptically on CΓC_{\Gamma}. Then Min⁡(g)=Min⁡(gk)\mathrm{Min}(g)=\mathrm{Min}(g^{k}) for every k≥1k\geq 1 and g∈AΓg\in A_{\Gamma}.

Proof.

Stabilisers of points of CΓC_{\Gamma} are parabolic subgroups of AΓA_{\Gamma} by construction. Since parabolic subgroups of two-dimensional Artin groups are closed under taking roots by Theorem 5.10, the result follows immediately. ∎

Proof of Theorem 5.17.

Let s,ts,t be two elements of SS, and let us first assume that s,ts,t belong to a dihedral parabolic subgroup HH with label ma​bm_{ab}. Since HH contains an index ma​b′m_{ab}^{\prime} subgroup that is of the form ℤ×Fk\mathbb{Z}\times F_{k} for some k≥1k\geq 1, it follows that sma​b′s^{m_{ab}^{\prime}} and tma​b′t^{m_{ab}^{\prime}} either commute or a generate a free subgroup. Otherwise, s,ts,t do not belong to a dihedral parabolic subgroup, and it follows from Theorem 5.3 that s3,t3s^{3},t^{3} either commute or generate a free subgroup. In any case, it follows that sms^{m} and tmt^{m} either commute or generate a free subgroup. If for one pair of elements s,t∈Ss,t\in S, we have that sms^{m} and tmt^{m} generate a free subgroup, we are done. So, let us assume by contradiction that for every pair s,ts,t of distinct elements of SS, the elements sms^{m} and tmt^{m} commute.

First, suppose that some element s0∈Ss_{0}\in S acts loxodromically on CΓC_{\Gamma}, hence on DΓD_{\Gamma}, which we think of as endowed with its CAT⁡(−1)\operatorname{CAT}(-1) metric.
