In particular, s0s_{0} admits a unique axis L⊂DΓL\subset D_{\Gamma}. Let s∈Ss\in S with s≠s0s\neq s_{0}. Since sms^{m} and s0ms_{0}^{m} commute, it follows that either ss is loxodromic with the same axis LL as s0s_{0}, or ss is elliptic with fixed-point set Min⁡(s)=Min⁡(sm)\mathrm{Min}(s)=\mathrm{Min}(s^{m}) a standard tree containing LL. Note in particular that there exists a unique standard tree of DΓD_{\Gamma} containing LL by [42]*Corollary 2.18 (Note that this result, and the others from [42] used in this proof, are stated for large-type Artin groups, but the reader can check that the proof holds more generally for two-dimensional Artin groups as their proof only use the fact that the Deligne complex admits a CAT⁡(0)\operatorname{CAT}(0) metric). Thus, either all elements of SS act loxodromically on DΓD_{\Gamma} with axis LL, or there exists a unique standard tree TT such that the minset of every element of SS is contained in TT. In the former case, we get that every s∈Ss\in S, hence ⟨S⟩=AΓ\langle S\rangle=A_{\Gamma}, is contained in StabAΓ⁡(L)\operatorname{Stab}_{A_{\Gamma}}(L). As the pointwise stabiliser of LL is either infinite cyclic (if it is contained in a standard tree) or trivial (otherwise) by [42]*Corollary 2.17, it follows that AΓA_{\Gamma} is virtually abelian, a contradiction. In the latter case, it follows from [42]*Lemma 2.15 that every element of SS, and hence ⟨S⟩=AΓ\langle S\rangle=A_{\Gamma}, is contained in StabAΓ⁡(T)\operatorname{Stab}_{A_{\Gamma}}(T), which is of the form ℤ×Fk\mathbb{Z}\times F_{k} by [54]*Lemma 4.5. Since AΓA_{\Gamma} is not abelian, it follows that some pair of elements of SS generates a non-abelian free subgroup, contradicting our assumption.

Now suppose that all elements s∈Ss\in S act elliptically on CΓC_{\Gamma}. This implies that for every pair, the minsets Min⁡(sm)=Min⁡(s)\mathrm{Min}(s^{m})=\mathrm{Min}(s) and Min⁡(tm)=Min⁡(t)\mathrm{Min}(t^{m})=\mathrm{Min}(t) have a non-empty intersection, otherwise some large powers would generate a free subgroup by [55]*Proposition C. Since the fixed-point sets Min⁡(s)\mathrm{Min}(s) are convex subcomplexes of CΓC_{\Gamma} and pairwise intersect, the Helly property for CAT(0) cube complexes [61]*Theorem 2.2 implies that there exists a vertex of DΓD_{\Gamma} fixed by all s∈Ss\in S, hence by ⟨S⟩=AΓ\langle S\rangle=A_{\Gamma}. Thus, AΓA_{\Gamma} is a dihedral Artin group, a contradiction. ∎

6. Examples, additional applications, and questions

We now define a class of groups, starting with hyperbolic groups and closed under several operations, such that all groups in the class satisfy the power alternative (uniformly). The goal is to recover several existing examples in a unified way; one could probably define such a class of groups more generally, in terms of acylindrical actions on hyperbolic complexes such that the stabilisers of simplices are in the class and satisfy suitable “rotation” conditions along the lines of [32] or [12]. However, in the interest of concreteness, we content ourselves with a less general approach sufficient for our favourite examples.

We refer the reader to, for instance, [23] for the definition of relative hyperbolicity of a pair (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}), where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a set of subgroups of the finitely generated group GG. We also recall:

Definition 6.1 (Acylindricity).

Given a metric space XX and a group GG, an action G→Isom⁡(X)G\to\operatorname{Isom}(X) is acylindrical if for each ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 there exist R⁡(ε),N⁡(ε)<∞R(\varepsilon),N(\varepsilon)<\infty such that

|{g∈G:dX​(x,g​x)≤ε​and ​dX​(y,g​y)≤ε}|≤N⁡(ε)|\{g\in G:d_{X}(x,gx)\leq\varepsilon\ \text{and }d_{X}(y,gy)\leq\varepsilon\}|\leq N(\varepsilon)

for all x,y∈Xx,y\in X with dX​(x,y)>R⁡(ε)d_{X}(x,y)>R(\varepsilon). The functions RR and NN are the acylindricity parameters.

We are usually interested in the case where XX is a hyperbolic geodesic space; in this setting the notion was defined in [24]. In the case where XX is a simplicial tree, the notion of acylindricity of the GG–action was formulated earlier, and equivalently, by Sela in [62]: there exist K,c∈ℤ≥0K,c\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that if v,w∈Vert⁡(X)v,w\in\operatorname{Vert}(X) satisfy dX​(v,w)>Kd_{X}(v,w)>K, then |StabG⁡(v)∩StabG⁡(w)|≤c|\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(v)\cap\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(w)|\leq c.

Remark 6.2.

To facilitate quantitative statements about the power alternative, we introduce some notation. Let GG be a group. The power alternative function PAG:G2→ℕ≥1∪{∞}\mathrm{PA}_{G}:G^{2}\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\} is defined as follows. Given g,h∈Gg,h\in G, let PAG​(g,h)\mathrm{PA}_{G}(g,h) be the smallest positive integer nn such that either [gn,hn]=1[g^{n},h^{n}]=1 or ⟨gn,hn⟩≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle\cong F_{2}. If no such nn exists, then PAG​(g,h)=∞\mathrm{PA}_{G}(g,h)=\infty. Hence GG satisfies the power alternative if and only if PAG​(g,h)<∞\mathrm{PA}_{G}(g,h)<\infty for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G. We also let PA⁡(G)=supg,h∈GPAG​(g,h)\mathrm{PA}(G)=\sup_{g,h\in G}\mathrm{PA}_{G}(g,h). So, GG satisfies the uniform power alternative if PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty. Finally, if 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a family of groups, we let PA⁡(𝒫)=supP∈𝒫PA⁡(P)\mathrm{PA}(\mathcal{P})=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathrm{PA}(P).

Definition 6.3 (the classes 𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{PA} and 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA}).

We define classes 𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{PA} and 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA} of groups as follows. First, let 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜0\mathcal{UPA}_{0} be the class of finitely generated groups GG that fit into an exact sequence Z↪G↠HZ\hookrightarrow G\twoheadrightarrow H where HH is a hyperbolic group and ZZ is free abelian of rank at most 11 that is central in GG. Define 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA} to be the smallest class of finitely generated groups that satisfies all of the following closure properties:

  1. (1)

    𝒰​𝒫​𝒜0⊂𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA}_{0}\subset\mathcal{UPA}.

  2. (2)

    If G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA} and [G′:G]<∞[G^{\prime}:G]<\infty then G′∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{UPA}.

  3. (3)

    If G,G′∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G,G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{UPA} then G×G′∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\times G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{UPA}.

  4. (4)

    Let GG admit a cocompact acylindrical action on a tree TT such that all vertex stabilisers belong to 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA} and are closed under roots, i.e. for g∈Gg\in G and v∈Tv\in T, if gn​v=vg^{n}v=v for some n≠0n\neq 0, then g​v=vgv=v. Then G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA}.

  5. (5)

    Let Γ\Gamma be a finite simplicial graph, for each v∈Vert⁡(Γ)v\in\operatorname{Vert}(\Gamma) let GvG_{v} be a nontrivial group, and let GG be the graph product of {Gv:v∈Γ}\{G_{v}:v\in\Gamma\}. If each Gv∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G_{v}\in\mathcal{UPA}, then G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA}.

  6. (6)

    If GG is hyperbolic relative to a finite collection 𝒫\mathcal{P} of subgroups and each H∈𝒫H\in\mathcal{P} belongs to 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA}, then G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA}.

The larger class 𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{PA} is defined identically, replacing 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA} with 𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{PA}, except condition (4) changes to:

  1. (iv)

    GG acts on a tree TT with the stabilisation property, and all stabilisers of points in Vert⁡(T)∪∂T\operatorname{Vert}(T)\cup\partial T belong to 𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{PA}.

The point of Definition 6.3 is just to enable a succinct statement of the following:

Theorem 6.4 (omnibus combination theorem).

If G∈𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{PA}, then GG satisfies the power alternative. If G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA}, then GG satisfies the uniform power alternative.

Proof.

Theorem 6.5 and Lemma 6.6 below show that G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜0G\in\mathcal{UPA}_{0} implies PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty. Lemma 2.2 and Lemma 2.4 show that satisfying the [uniform] power alternative is stable under passing to finite index supergroups and taking direct products. Theorem A implies that groups GG as in condition (iv) satisfy the non-uniform power alternative.

If GG is hyperbolic relative to a finite collection of groups HH such that PA⁡(H)<∞\mathrm{PA}(H)<\infty, then PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty by Theorem 6.9. In order to apply the theorem, we need to know that there is a bound on the orders of torsion elements of GG, but this property holds for hyperbolic groups and persists under all of the operations in Definition 6.3.

Now, suppose GG acts acylindrically and cocompactly on a tree TT, acylindrically and cocompactly, and the vertex stabilisers GvG_{v} are all closed under roots and satisfy PA⁡(Gv)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G_{v})<\infty. Then Proposition 6.8 below implies PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty (with the corresponding observation about torsion).

The statement about graph products follows from [7]*Corollary 1.5. This concludes the proof. ∎

It remains to prove the results from the proof of Theorem 6.4, which we do in the next few subsections.

6.1. Central extensions of hyperbolic groups

The first result is well-known and can be recovered from arguments in [39], but we will recover it as a special case of a more general statement:

Theorem 6.5.

Let GG be a group equipped with a finite generating set such that the resulting word metric on GG is δ\delta–hyperbolic. Then there exists a natural number n⁡(G)n(G) such that PA⁡(G)≤n⁡(G)\mathrm{PA}(G)\leq n(G). More precisely, there exists a positive integer n=n⁡(G)n=n(G) such that for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G of infinite order:

  1. (1)

    if gg and hh share a limit point in ∂G\partial G, then both their limit points coincide and ⟨g,h⟩G\langle g,h\rangle_{G} contains a finite index ℤ\mathbb{Z} subgroup containing gng^{n} and hnh^{n}, and otherwise,

  2. (2)

    if gg and hh do not share any points in ∂G\partial G, then ⟨gn,hn⟩G≅F2\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G}\cong F_{2}.

Proof.

This is the special case of Theorem 6.9 where 𝒫={{1}}\mathcal{P}=\{\{1\}\}. ∎

Lemma 6.6.

Let HH be a hyperbolic group and let

1→ℤ→G→H→11\to\mathbb{Z}\to G\to H\to 1

be an extension. Then GG satisfies the uniform power alternative.

Proof.

Let g,h∈Gg,h\in G and let g¯,h¯\bar{g},\bar{h} denote their images in HH. Choose n≥1n\geq 1 such that ⟨g¯n,h¯n⟩H\langle\bar{g}^{n},\bar{h}^{n}\rangle_{H} is either nonabelian free or cyclic, using Theorem 6.5. In the former case, ⟨gn,hn⟩G\langle g^{n},h^{n}\rangle_{G} is again free; in the latter, ⟨g2​n,h2​n⟩G\langle g^{2n},h^{2n}\rangle_{G} abelian since the preimage of ⟨g¯2​n,h¯2​n⟩H\langle\bar{g}^{2n},\bar{h}^{2n}\rangle_{H} in GG is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} or ℤ\mathbb{Z}. ∎

6.2. Actions on hyperbolic spaces

In this section, we prove the following two results, whose proofs we postpone until after some lemmas.

Notation 6.7.

In order to lighten the notations, in the rest of this section we will simply write as GvG_{v} the stabiliser StabG⁡(v)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(v) of a vertex vv of TT.

Proposition 6.8.

Let GG act acylindrically and cocompactly on a tree TT. Suppose that PA⁡(Gv)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G_{v})<\infty and GvG_{v} is closed under roots, for each v∈Vert⁡(T)v\in\operatorname{Vert}(T). Then PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty and GG has a bound on the orders of torsion elements.

The power alternative for GG acting acylindrically on a tree is Corollary 4.1, but below, we will argue slightly differently to get the uniform version.

In the next theorem, we consider a relatively hyperbolic pair (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}). Given a finite generating set SS of GG, the coned-off Cayley graph Cay⁡(G,S,𝒫)\operatorname{Cay}(G,S;\mathcal{P}) is obtained from the Cayley graph Cay⁡(G,S)\operatorname{Cay}(G,S) by coning off each coset g​P,P∈𝒫,g∈GgP,\ P\in\mathcal{P},g\in G; see [23] for details.

Theorem 6.9.

Let GG be a finitely generated group that is hyperbolic relative to a finite collection 𝒫\mathcal{P} of subgroups. Let δ≥0\delta\geq 0 be such that GG admits a finite generating set SS such that Cay⁡(G,S,𝒫)\operatorname{Cay}(G,S;\mathcal{P}) is δ\delta–hyperbolic.

Then GG satisfies the power alternative provided each H∈𝒫H\in\mathcal{P} does. Moreover, suppose that there is a bound B<∞B<\infty on the orders of finite-order elements of subgroups in 𝒫\mathcal{P} and PA⁡(𝒫)<∞\mathrm{PA}(\mathcal{P})<\infty. Then PA⁡(G)\mathrm{PA}(G) is bounded in terms of PA⁡(𝒫),B,δ\mathrm{PA}(\mathcal{P}),B,\delta, and the acylindricity parameters of the GG–action on Cay⁡(G,S,𝒫)\operatorname{Cay}(G,S;\mathcal{P}).

In particular, if GG has bounded torsion, then GG satisfies the power alternative uniformly if 𝒫\mathcal{P} does.

We now analyse certain two-generated subgroups of an acylindrically hyperbolic group, in order to unify the proofs of the above two statements. The following is similar to arguments in, for instance, [1].

Fix a group GG and a δ\delta–hyperbolic graph XX, whose graph metric we call dXd_{X}. Suppose that GG acts by acylindrically by isometries on XX, with R:ℝ≥0→ℝ≥0R:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} and N:ℝ≥0→ℤ≥0N:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} as in Definition 6.1.

Given such an action, we say that a quantity is uniform if it depends on δ\delta and the functions (R,N)(R,N) but not on any particular points in XX or elements of GG.

Given g∈Gg\in G, let

A⁡(g)={x∈X:dX​(x,g​x)≤infy∈XdX​(y,g​y)+10​δ}.A(g)=\{x\in X:d_{X}(x,gx)\leq\inf_{y\in X}d_{X}(y,gy)+10\delta\}.

Acylindricity provides a uniform n1<∞n_{1}<\infty such that, for all g∈Gg\in G, one of the following holds:

  • •

    gg is loxodromic on XX. In this case, A⁡(g)A(g) is n1n_{1}–quasiconvex and (n1,n1)(n_{1},n_{1})–quasiisometric, in the subspace metric, to a line. Moreover, the unique maximal elementary subgroup E⁡(g)≤GE(g)\leq G containing gg is the stabiliser of A⁡(g)A(g). (See [32, Lemma 6.5].)

  • •

    ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle has bounded orbits in XX. In this case, there exists x∈Xx\in X such that diamX​(⟨g⟩⋅x)≤5​δ\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\langle g\rangle\cdot x)\leq 5\delta (see, for instance, [25, Lemma III.Γ\Gamma.3.3]). So either gg has order at most N⁡(15​δ)N(15\delta) or diamX​(A⁡(g))≤R⁡(15​δ)\mathrm{diam}_{X}(A(g))\leq R(15\delta), and we can assume, by uniformly enlarging n1n_{1}, that R⁡(15​δ)≤n1R(15\delta)\leq n_{1} and that A⁡(g)A(g) is n1n_{1}–quasiconvex.

Now fix g∈Gg\in G. Observe:

Lemma 6.10.

If gg has order at most N⁡(15​δ)N(15\delta), then PAG​(g,h)\mathrm{PA}_{G}(g,h) is bounded uniformly, for any h∈Gh\in G.

So assume that gg has order more than N⁡(15​δ)N(15\delta), and hence A⁡(g)A(g) has diameter at most n1n_{1} when gg has bounded orbits in XX. For g∈Gg\in G loxodromic on XX, fix x0∈Xx_{0}\in X and let τ⁡(g)=limn→∞dX​(x0,gn​x0)/n\tau(g)=\lim_{n\to\infty}d_{X}(x_{0},g^{n}x_{0})/n. Since the action is acylindrical, there is a uniform τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 such that τ⁡(g)≥τ0\tau(g)\geq\tau_{0} whenever gg is loxodromic, as shown in [24].

Definition 6.11.

Given g∈Gg\in G, let πg:X→2A⁡(g)\pi_{g}:X\to 2^{A(g)} be the coarse closest-point projection, i.e. for x∈Xx\in X, let

πg​(x)={y∈A⁡(g):dX​(x,y)≤d⁡(x,A⁡(g))+1}.\pi_{g}(x)=\{y\in A(g):d_{X}(x,y)\leq d(x,A(g))+1\}.

Since XX is δ\delta–hyperbolic and A⁡(g)A(g) is n1n_{1}–quasiconvex, there is a uniform constant CC with the following properties that together say πg\pi_{g} is a uniformly coarsely lipschitz coarse retraction:

  • •

    diamX​(πg​(x))≤C\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\pi_{g}(x))\leq C for all x∈Xx\in X.

  • •

    dX​(πg​(x),πg​(y))≤C​dX​(x,y)+Cd_{X}(\pi_{g}(x),\pi_{g}(y))\leq Cd_{X}(x,y)+C for all x,y∈Xx,y\in X.

  • •

    dX​(a,πg​(a))≤Cd_{X}(a,\pi_{g}(a))\leq C for all a∈A⁡(g)a\in A(g).

Moreover, if h∈Gh\in G, note that A⁡(h​g​h−1)=h​A​(g)A(hgh^{-1})=hA(g), and for all x∈Xx\in X we have h⋅πg​(x)=πh​g​h−1​(h⋅x)h\cdot\pi_{g}(x)=\pi_{hgh^{-1}}(h\cdot x). (These are standard facts about coarse projection to quasiconvex subspaces of a hyperbolic space.)

Lemma 6.12.

There exists a uniform constant C1C_{1} such that the following holds. Let g,h∈Gg,h\in G have order at least N⁡(15​δ)N(15\delta) and let τ=min⁡{τ⁡(g),τ⁡(h)}\tau=\min\{\tau(g),\tau(h)\}. Then all of the following hold:

  1. (1)

    diamX​(πh​(A⁡(g​h​g−1)))=diamX​(πh​(g​A​(h)))≤C1​τ​(h)+C1\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\pi_{h}(A(ghg^{-1})))=\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\pi_{h}(gA(h)))\leq C_{1}\tau(h)+C_{1} unless dHaus​(A⁡(h),g​A​(h))≤C1.d_{\textup{Haus}}(A(h),gA(h))\leq C_{1}.

  2. (2)

    diamX​(πh​(A⁡(g)))≤C1​τ+C1\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\pi_{h}(A(g)))\leq C_{1}\tau+C_{1} unless dHaus​(A⁡(g),A⁡(h))≤C1.d_{\textup{Haus}}(A(g),A(h))\leq C_{1}.

  3. (3)

    If dX​(A⁡(h),g​A​(h))>C1d_{X}(A(h),gA(h))>C_{1}, then diamX​(πh​(g​A​(h)))≤C1\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\pi_{h}(gA(h)))\leq C_{1}, and the same holds replacing g​A​(h)gA(h) with A⁡(g)A(g).

Proof.

The first assertion follows from the second, by replacing gg with g​h​g−1ghg^{-1}. Our assumption on the order implies the second assertion immediately if gg or hh has finite order, so we can assume they have infinite order. Using uniform quasiconvexity of the uniform quasi-axes A⁡(g),A⁡(h)A(g),A(h), acylindricity, and a thin quadrilateral argument, we obtain the third assertion, along with the conclusion that diamX​(πh​(A⁡(g)))≤C1​τ+C1\mathrm{diam}_{X}(\pi_{h}(A(g)))\leq C_{1}\tau+C_{1} unless A⁡(g)A(g) and A⁡(h)A(h) are at finite Hausdorff distance, as required. (See also [32, Section 6].) ∎

Lemma 6.12 and a standard thin quadrilateral argument give:

Lemma 6.13 (“Behrstock inequality”).

There exists a uniform constant C2C_{2} such that the following holds. Let h∈Gh\in G be loxodromic and let x∈Xx\in X. Then the following hold for all g∈Gg\in G:

  • •

    Suppose that E⁡(h)≠E⁡(g​h​g−1)E(h)\neq E(ghg^{-1}). Then dX​(πh​(x),πh​(g​A​(h)))>C2d_{X}(\pi_{h}(x),\pi_{h}(gA(h)))>C_{2} implies

    dX​(πg​h​g−1​(x),πg​h​g−1​(A⁡(h)))≤C2.d_{X}(\pi_{ghg^{-1}}(x),\pi_{ghg^{-1}}(A(h)))\leq C_{2}.
  • •

    Suppose that E⁡(g)≠E⁡(h)E(g)\neq E(h). Then dX​(πh​(x),πh​(A⁡(g)))>C2d_{X}(\pi_{h}(x),\pi_{h}(A(g)))>C_{2} implies dX​(πg​(x),πg​(A⁡(h)))≤C2d_{X}(\pi_{g}(x),\pi_{g}(A(h)))\leq C_{2}.

Now we study the subgroup of GG generated by uniform powers of g,h∈Gg,h\in G with hh loxodromic.

Lemma 6.14 (acylindrical, loxodromic-loxodromic).

There exists a uniform p∈ℤ>0p\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} such that for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G that are both loxodromic on XX, either ⟨gp,hp⟩≅F2\langle g^{p},h^{p}\rangle\cong F_{2} or gp,hpg^{p},h^{p} commute.

Lemma 6.15 (acylindrical, elliptic-loxodromic).

There exists uniform p∈ℤ>0p\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} such that the following holds. Suppose that g∈Gg\in G is elliptic on XX and h∈Gh\in G is loxodromic. Then either ⟨gp,hp⟩≅⟨gp⟩∗⟨hp⟩\langle g^{p},h^{p}\rangle\cong\langle g^{p}\rangle*\langle h^{p}\rangle or ⟨g⟩∩E⁡(h)≠{1}\langle g\rangle\cap E(h)\neq\{1\}.

Then A⁡(g)A(g) has uniformly bounded diameter, so up to uniformly enlarging C1C_{1}, we can assume A⁡(g)A(g) and πh​(A​(g))\pi_{h}(A(g)) both have diameter at most C1C_{1}. Sh={x∈X:dX​(πh​(x),πh​(A⁡(g)))>L}.S_{h}=\{x\in X:d_{X}(\pi_{h}(x),\pi_{h}(A(g)))>L\}.

Let Sg=X−ShS_{g}=X-S_{h}.

In the remainder of the argument, we will impose additional uniform conditions on LL as we go. So A⁡(g)∩gk​Sh=∅A(g)\cap g^{k}S_{h}=\varnothing, whence gk​Sh⊊Sgg^{k}S_{h}\subsetneq S_{g}. Hence the ping-pong lemma implies ⟨gp,hp⟩≅⟨gp⟩∗⟨hp⟩\langle g^{p},h^{p}\rangle\cong\langle g^{p}\rangle*\langle h^{p}\rangle. ∎

Remark 6.16.

Arguments similar to the ones in the preceding lemmas also occur in, for instance, [1, Proposition 2.1] and [44, Lemma 2.3].

Now we consider the case of a relatively hyperbolic pair (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}).

Proof of Theorem 6.9.

Let G^=Cay⁡(G,S,𝒫)\widehat{G}=\operatorname{Cay}(G,S;\mathcal{P}) be a coned-off Cayley graph and choose δ\delta so that G^\widehat{G} is δ\delta–hyperbolic. We let dd be the word-metric on GG associated to SS and let d^\hat{d} be the graph metric on G^\widehat{G}. The natural action of GG on G^\widehat{G} is acylindrical [56, Theorem 5.4]. Now apply Lemma 6.14 and Lemma 6.15 to obtain a uniform pp such that if g,h∈Gg,h\in G and at least one is loxodromic, then one of the following holds: ⟨gp,hp⟩≅⟨gp⟩∗⟨hp⟩\langle g^{p},h^{p}\rangle\cong\langle g^{p}\rangle*\langle h^{p}\rangle, or [gp,hp]=1[g^{p},h^{p}]=1, or hh is loxodromic, gg is elliptic, and E⁡(h)∩⟨g⟩≠{1}E(h)\cap\langle g\rangle\neq\{1\}.

In either of the first two cases, we are done, so assume the third holds. For the non-uniform conclusion, we can always assume g,hg,h have infinite order, so we are done since E⁡(h)E(h) is virtually cyclic. For the uniform case, we argue as follows. First, our hypotheses imply that gg having finite order implies that it has bounded order, so we can assume gg has infinite order, is elliptic, and gn∈E⁡(h)g^{n}\in E(h) for some n≠0n\neq 0. Then by [56, Lemma 6.8], nn can be chosen (non-uniformly) so that gn∈⟨h⟩g^{n}\in\langle h\rangle, which contradicts ellipticity of gg (since hh is loxodromic), so we are done.

Hence it remains to consider the case where ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle and ⟨h⟩\langle h\rangle both have bounded orbits on G^\widehat{G}. We will use a projection argument analogous to the one in the proof of Lemma 6.14, except with peripheral cosets replacing axes. For each P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} and a∈Ga\in G, let πa​P:G→a​P\pi_{aP}:G\to aP be the coarse closest-point projection from [64, Section 1.1]. Note that πa​P​(a​x)=a​πP​(x)\pi_{aP}(ax)=a\pi_{P}(x) for all a,x∈Ga,x\in G.

Suppose that a,b∈Ga,b\in G and P,Q∈𝒫P,Q\in\mathcal{P} satisfy a​P≠b​QaP\neq bQ. Then there exists CC, depending only on (G,d)(G,d) and 𝒫\mathcal{P} such that πa​Pg​(b​Ph)\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}) and πb​Ph​(a​Pg)\pi_{bP_{h}}(aP_{g}) have dd–diameter bounded by CC; this follows from [64, Lemma 1.9, Lemma 1.10, Lemma 1.15]. Also, up to uniformly enlarging CC, [64, Lemma 1.13, Lemma 1.15] implies: if x∈Gx\in G satisfies d⁡(πb​Q​(x),πb​Q​(a​P))>Cd(\pi_{bQ}(x),\pi_{bQ}(aP))>C, then d⁡(πa​P​(b​Q),πa​P​(x))≤Cd(\pi_{aP}(bQ),\pi_{aP}(x))\leq C. Let L=100​CL=100C.

Now fix g,h∈Gg,h\in G having bounded orbits in G^\widehat{G}. By replacing gg and hh by uniform positive powers, we can assume that there exist Pg,Ph∈𝒫P_{g},P_{h}\in\mathcal{P} such that g∈a​Pg​a−1g\in aP_{g}a^{-1} and h∈b​Ph​b−1h\in bP_{h}b^{-1} for some a,b∈Ga,b\in G. Since 𝒫\mathcal{P} is almost-malnormal [23], we can assume a​PgaP_{g} and b​PhbP_{h} are unique. By the hypothesis about the power alternative in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we can assume a​Pg≠b​PhaP_{g}\neq bP_{h} (i.e., if g,hg,h belong to a common peripheral subgroup, then whichever of the uniform or non-uniform power alternatives is assumed for peripherals can be applied to the given g,hg,h). We can also assume that gg and hh have infinite order since, in the case where we are concerned with the uniform power alternative, we have assumed a uniform bound on the orders of torsion elements.

Since πa​Pg​(b​Ph)\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}) has diameter at most CC, there is a [uniform] pp such that

d⁡(gk​p​πa​Pg​(b​Ph),πa​Pg​(b​Ph))>100​Ld(g^{kp}\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}),\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}))>100L

for k∈ℤ−{0}k\in\mathbb{Z}-\{0\}, and the same holds reversing the roles of a​PgaP_{g} and b​PhbP_{h} and replacing gpg^{p} with hph^{p}.

Let Xg=πa​Pg−1​(a​Pg−NLG​(πa​Pg​(b​Ph)))X_{g}=\pi_{aP_{g}}^{-1}(aP_{g}-N_{L}^{G}(\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}))) and let Xh=πb​Ph−1​(b​Ph−NLG​(πb​Ph​(a​Pg)))X_{h}=\pi_{bP_{h}}^{-1}(bP_{h}-N^{G}_{L}(\pi_{bP_{h}}(aP_{g}))). If x∈Xhx\in X_{h}, then d⁡(πb​Ph​(x),πb​Ph​(a​Pg))>Ld(\pi_{bP_{h}}(x),\pi_{bP_{h}}(aP_{g}))>L, so d⁡(πa​Pg​(x),πa​Pg​(b​Ph))≤Cd(\pi_{aP_{g}}(x),\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}))\leq C. Hence Xg∩Xh=∅X_{g}\cap X_{h}=\varnothing. Moreover, for k≠0k\neq 0, we have d⁡(gp​k​πa​Pg​(x),πa​Pg​(b​Ph))>100​L−2​C>Ld(g^{pk}\pi_{aP_{g}}(x),\pi_{aP_{g}}(bP_{h}))>100L-2C>L, so gk​p​x∈Xgg^{kp}x\in X_{g}. In fact, we have shown gk​p​Xh⊊Xgg^{kp}X_{h}\subsetneq X_{g} for k≠0k\neq 0. Similarly, hk​p​Xg⊊Xhh^{kp}X_{g}\subsetneq X_{h} for k≠0k\neq 0. The ping-pong lemma then implies ⟨gp,hp⟩≅F2\langle g^{p},h^{p}\rangle\cong F_{2}. ∎

Now we turn to actions on trees.

Proof of Proposition 6.8.

Let GG act acylindrically and cocompactly on the tree TT. Suppose that vertex stabilisers are closed under roots. This has the following consequence: let g∈Gg\in G have finite order. Then gg is elliptic, so let vv be a vertex with g​v=vgv=v. Since gg has finite order, there exists n≠0n\neq 0 such that gng^{n} acts on TT trivially, so since vertex groups are closed under roots, gg acts on TT trivially and hence belongs to the unique maximal finite normal subgroup of GG; see [32, Theorem 2.23]. This gives the bound on orders of torsion elements.

Fix g,h∈Gg,h\in G with hh loxodromic. Since GG acts on TT acylindrically by hypothesis, we can apply Lemma 6.14 and Lemma 6.15 to obtain a uniform constant pp such that either [gp,hp]=1[g^{p},h^{p}]=1, or gg is elliptic and gp∈E⁡(h)g^{p}\in E(h), or ⟨gp,hp⟩≅⟨gp⟩∗⟨hp⟩\langle g^{p},h^{p}\rangle\cong\langle g^{p}\rangle*\langle h^{p}\rangle. If g,hg,h have infinite order, we are done (using [56, Lemma 6.8] to handle the case where gg has a power in E⁡(h)E(h)). But if gg has finite order, then either we conclude immediately, or, in the case where we require uniformity, we use the bound on torsion elements of vertex groups.

Hence it remains to consider the case where each of gg and hh is elliptic. Since vertex stabilisers are closed under roots by hypothesis, Fix⁡(g)=Fix∞⁡(g)\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g) and the same is true replacing gg with hh. Therefore, if Fix∞⁡(g)∩Fix∞⁡(h)≠∅\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(h)\neq\varnothing then Fix⁡(g)∩Fix⁡(h)≠∅\operatorname{Fix}(g)\cap\operatorname{Fix}(h)\neq\varnothing, and applying our hypotheses to the stabiliser of any vertex fixed by both gg and hh concludes the proof. On the other hand, if Fix∞⁡(g)∩Fix∞⁡(h)=∅\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g)\cap\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(h)=\varnothing, Lemma 3.7 shows ⟨g,h⟩≅F2\langle g,h\rangle\cong F_{2}. ∎

6.2.1. Closure under roots and a generalisation

Let GG act acylindrically on the tree TT without inversions. We saw above that for any elliptic g∈Gg\in G, the subtrees Fix⁡(g)⊂Fix∞⁡(g)\operatorname{Fix}(g)\subset\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g) have uniformly bounded diameter. However, this is insufficient to conclude that there is a uniform power pp such that gpg^{p} fixes Fix∞⁡(g)\operatorname{Fix}^{\infty}(g) pointwise, which is needed in the “elliptic-elliptic” case of the proof of Proposition 6.8. The extra “closure under roots” property is a bit stronger than is needed to ensure this, but it is a useful condition because it is easy to verify in our examples of interest:

Lemma 6.17.

Let GG act on the tree TT. For v∈Vert⁡(T)v\in\operatorname{Vert}(T), let ℰv\mathcal{E}_{v} be the set of edges of TT incident to vv and let ρv:Gv→Gv/K⁡(Gv)\rho_{v}:G_{v}\to G_{v}/K(G_{v}) be the natural quotient, where K⁡(Gv)K(G_{v}) is the kernel of the GvG_{v}–action on ℰv\mathcal{E}_{v}. Suppose that for all v∈Vert⁡(T)v\in\operatorname{Vert}(T), the collection {ρv​(Ge):e∈ℰv}\{\rho_{v}(G_{e}):e\in\mathcal{E}_{v}\} is malnormal in Gv/K⁡(Gv)G_{v}/K(G_{v}) and the latter group is torsion-free. Then each vertex-stabiliser GwG_{w} is closed under roots.

Proof.

Let g∈Gg\in G and suppose that gn​w=wg^{n}w=w for some n>0n>0 and w∈Vert⁡(T)w\in\operatorname{Vert}(T). Then there is a vertex vv with g​v=vgv=v. Let γ\gamma be the geodesic from vv to ww, which we can assume has length at least 11, for otherwise we are done. Let ee be the initial edge of γ\gamma. We first show that g∈Geg\in G_{e}. To this end, note that gng^{n} fixes vv and ww, so it fixes the geodesic [v,w][v,w] pointwise, and hence gn∈Geg^{n}\in G_{e}. Thus, for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, gn∈Ggi​eg^{n}\in G_{g^{i}e}, so ρv​(gn)∈ρv​(g)i​ρv​(Ge)​ρv​(g)−i\rho_{v}(g^{n})\in\rho_{v}(g)^{i}\rho_{v}(G_{e})\rho_{v}(g)^{-i} for all ii, and the malnormality and torsion hypotheses imply g∈K⁡(Gv)g\in K(G_{v}) and hence g∈Geg\in G_{e}. Thus g∈Gv′g\in G_{v^{\prime}} where v′v^{\prime} is the terminal point of ee, so since dT​(v′,w)<dT​(v,w)d_{T}(v^{\prime},w)<d_{T}(v,w), it follows by induction that g∈Gwg\in G_{w}, as required. ∎

6.3. Examples

Theorem 6.4 recovers various examples, some of which were known by other means.

Corollary 6.18.

Let MM be a closed connected oriented 33–manifold. Then PA⁡(π1​M)<∞\mathrm{PA}(\pi_{1}M)<\infty unless MM has a Nil or Sol piece in its prime decomposition.

Proof.

By the prime decomposition theorem, [34, Theorem 0.1] (see also [8, Theorem 9.2], [19, Corollary E]), [40, Lemma 3.12, Lemma 3.13], Lemma 6.17, and Theorem 6.4, it suffices to consider the case where either MM is geometric, or MM is a large Seifert fibred manifold with toral boundary (large means that the base orbifold has negative Euler characteristic). In the latter case, π1​M\pi_{1}M is a central extension of a hyperbolic group, and hence in 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA}. In the former, examining the eight geometries, either Theorem 6.4 applies, or MM is a Nil or Sol manifold. ∎

Remark 6.19.

Most cases of Corollary 6.18 were known by other means: we have already mentioned the 1979 result of Jaco-Shalen [48] when MM is, for instance, a finite-volume hyperbolic Haken manifold. The case where MM is hyperbolic is covered by the (classical) Theorem 6.5, and, more generally, the cases where π1​M\pi_{1}M is virtually special are covered by [9] since virtually special groups virtually embed in RAAGs [45]. The latter cases include hyperbolic 33–manifolds, graph manifolds that are either nonpositively-curved or have nonempty boundary, and mixed 33–manifolds [2][59][52][60].

Corollary 6.20.

Let FF be a finite-rank free group and let Φ∈Out⁡(F)\Phi\in\operatorname{Out}(F). Then the mapping torus G=F⋊ΦℤG=F\rtimes_{\Phi}\mathbb{Z} satisfies PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty.

Proof.

We will show that G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA}, from which the result follows by Theorem 6.4. By [33, Theorem 3.5], GG is hyperbolic relative to a finite collection of subgroups, each of which is the mapping torus of a polynomially-growing automorphism, it suffices to consider the case where Φ\Phi has polynomial growth. By [16, Proposition 3.5], up to replacing Φ\Phi by Φk\Phi^{k}, where k>0k>0 depends only on FF, we can assume that Φ\Phi is UPG in the sense of [16, Definition 3.10]. This has the effect of replacing GG by a bounded-index subgroup, which does not affect whether it is in 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA}. But once Φ\Phi is UPG, we can apply [4, Proposition 2.5] and [50, Lemma 5.2] to show that G∈𝒰​𝒫​𝒜G\in\mathcal{UPA}, as required. ∎

6.4. 𝒰​𝒫​𝒜\mathcal{UPA} versus hierarchical hyperbolicity

The class of hierarchically hyperbolic groups (HHGs) from [13] contains hyperbolic groups, and ℤ\mathbb{Z} central extensions of hyperbolic groups [43]. It is closed under graph products [15][58], and any group hyperbolic relative to a finite collection of HHGs is again an HHG [13]. Finite graphs of groups with HHG vertex groups for which the action on the Bass-Serre tree is acylindrical are again HHGs under fairly flexible quasiconvexity conditions on the edge groups [13][14]. While passing to finite-index supergroups need not preserve the property of being an HHG [58], the above facts, together with Theorem 6.4, provide many hierarchically hyperbolic groups GG with PA⁡(G)<∞\mathrm{PA}(G)<\infty. On the other hand, cocompact lattices in products of locally finite trees are HHGs [11], but it is open whether these always satisfy a power alternative, and there is some evidence (see [22]) against this.

Question 6.21.

Give natural conditions on a hierarchically hyperbolic group GG ensuring that it satisfies a (uniform) power alternative. Specifically, provided each standard product region (see [13, Section 5]) PP in GG has cocompact stabiliser in GG, does the power alternative hold in GG provided it holds in each product region subgroup StabG⁡(P)\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(P)?

We expect [11, Corollary 14.3], [36, Proposition 9.2], and [10, Remark 2.10] to be useful here. HHGs have uniformly bounded torsion [41] but need not be virtually torsion-free [47]. In many cases, like mapping class groups, hierarchical hyperbolicity comes from an acylindrical GG–action on a hyperbolic complex YY with features reminiscent of fine hyperbolic graphs for relatively hyperbolic groups [12].

Question 6.22.

Generalise Theorem 6.9 and Propsition 6.8 to prove the power alternative for groups acting acylindrically on hyperbolic simplicial complexes satisfying appropriate local conditions.

Such a statement would ideally be strong enough to recover a power alternative for mapping class groups, and give yet another proof for the result about graph products discussed in Remark 4.21. In the former case, one can imagine applying the desired generalisation to the action on the curve graph, while in the case of graph products, one might use the action on Valiunas’ contact graph [65].
